members.name: Maria Cantwell

just.ai_overall: She praises AI's potential in medicine, jobs, and competitiveness. She also repeatedly warns of serious harms to kids, consumers, health care, and security, and calls for guardrails, which makes her view balanced.
just.agi_pilled: She calls AI and quantum 'game changers' and says capabilities accelerate daily. She never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: She flags large-scale misuse risks such as autonomous cyberattacks, AI-designed bioweapons, and nuclear or biological weapons development. She cites a model 'breaking out of the sandbox'. She does not explicitly frame this as existential risk or loss of human control.
just.china_race: China competition recurs in her remarks on export controls, open models from China, and data centers. It is balanced with strong consumer-protection and safety themes rather than overriding them.
just.regulation: She backs mandatory independent testing, safety standards, and reporting of failures for frontier models. She also supports a federal framework and opposes preemption without strong guardrails. She stops short of calling for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Cantwell presents AI as a major opportunity for medicine, jobs, and U.S. competitiveness, but spends more time on risks to consumers, kids, health care, and national security. She presses for federal safety standards, independent testing of advanced models, and protection of state AI laws from weak preemption. China comes up mostly through export controls and tech leadership, and she cites cyber and bioweapon dangers without framing them as existential.

members.name: Amy Klobuchar

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's potential, such as health care advances and innovation, with serious harms like scams, deepfakes, and risks to kids. She describes it as 'heaven' and 'hell' and says guardrails decide which one we get.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is developing fast and will soon touch every part of life. Her statements otherwise stay on concrete harms such as scams, deepfakes, elections, and chatbots, with no AGI talk. She sarcastically questions a company's superintelligence claims.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are mostly everyday harms: scams, election deepfakes, kids and chatbots, privacy, and copyright. She briefly mentions infrastructure and cyberattack security, but never loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: China appears only once, when she asks witnesses who is winning the AI race. She also says America should lead on AI. The race is not a recurring frame in her policy arguments.
just.regulation: She backs substantial rules: the Thune risk-assessment bill with testing standards for high-risk AI, liability, a strong federal safety standard, and election and likeness laws. She opposes preempting state AI laws. She does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Klobuchar presents AI as a technology with real promise whose harms need 'rules of the road'. She focuses mainly on election deepfakes, voice-cloning scams, nonconsensual intimate images, kids and chatbots, and compensation for journalists and artists. She is a leading sponsor of bipartisan bills such as the NO FAKES and TAKE IT DOWN Acts and the Thune risk-based framework. She strongly opposes federal preemption of state AI laws, and she rarely discusses AGI, existential risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Bernard Sanders

just.ai_overall: He grants that AI and robotics "can help us in many ways" and cites healthcare benefits, but nearly all his statements stress job loss, billionaire power, surveillance and existential danger. Harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He repeatedly says AI will become smarter than humans "sooner or later" and may escape human control. He calls for a ban on superintelligence and compares it to nuclear weapons. He also calls AI the most transformational technology in human history.
just.x_risk: He calls AI an existential threat and says its danger is probably greater than nuclear weapons. He warns of loss of human control and possible extinction. He makes this a top priority, with a pause and a ban on superintelligence.
just.china_race: He rejects racing and calls for U.S.–China cooperation. He convened U.S. and Chinese scientists and urges Trump and Xi to negotiate an AI treaty, comparing it to Cold War arms control.
just.regulation: He backs a federal moratorium on AI data centers, a pause on advanced AI, and a permanent ban on superintelligence. He also backs public appointment of half of AI company boards and a public ownership stake in AI companies. He wants broad safety regulation comparable to food inspection.

members.summary: Sanders describes AI and robotics as the most transformative technologies in human history. He frames them mainly as a threat to workers and democracy when controlled by billionaire "oligarchs", and increasingly as an existential danger if superintelligence escapes human control. He pushes for a data center moratorium, a pause on advanced AI, a ban on superintelligence, public ownership stakes, and U.S.–China cooperation instead of a race. He grants some benefits, such as in healthcare, and says he is "not a Luddite".

members.name: Sheldon Whitehouse

just.ai_overall: His AI comments are mostly critical, focused on data centers' climate and electricity-cost impacts and on the political influence of AI/crypto donors. He acknowledges that AI and climate leadership can coexist (s8) and enjoys AI chatbots contradicting Trump, but harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or AI reshaping society at a civilizational scale. His remarks cover only data centers, energy, and specific uses.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: bias in law-enforcement AI, malicious deepfakes, electricity costs, pollution, and chatbot misinformation. None is framed as catastrophic or loss of control.
just.china_race: China competition is barely mentioned. The only race language is a passing remark that we need not choose between leading on AI and leading on climate, plus 'race to the bottom' on data center safety.
just.regulation: He backs targeted measures: closing gaps in criminal law on malicious AI fakery, safety standards for data centers, clean-power requirements, and the DISCLOSE Act. He does not describe a broad AI regulatory framework.

members.summary: Whitehouse mostly discusses AI through energy and politics. He criticizes data centers for straining grids, raising utility bills and polluting, and attacks AI, crypto and data-center donors as buying influence with Trump-aligned politicians. In hearings he asked practical questions about AI in law enforcement, medicine and deepfakes, and he often mocks AI chatbots on social media. He rarely addresses AGI, catastrophic risk or China.

members.name: John Barrasso

just.ai_overall: He frames AI as a strategic opportunity and a 'revolution' America must lead, while also flagging security and research-theft risks. The risks are treated as manageable through protection and energy supply.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'revolution' and says it is driving the biggest energy demand surge in decades, which suggests major transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He warns that AI could erode barriers to building a weapon, disease, or cyberattack, which is a large-scale misuse concern. He says nothing about loss of control.
just.china_race: He repeatedly describes an AI arms race with China that America 'cannot afford to lose', and uses it to argue for energy production. Race and security framing run through most of his AI statements.
just.regulation: He asks whether a light-handed regulatory structure is best, and his emphasis is on energy supply, research security and protecting data rather than new rules on AI companies. His proposals are narrow, such as blocking ChatGPT at DOE and requiring that public comments come from citizens. The evidence on general AI regulation is thin.

members.summary: Barrasso mostly discusses AI through China competition, energy demand and research security. He calls AI a revolution America must lead and describes an 'arms race' won by powering it with American energy. His concerns are mainly theft of technology, adversary influence and misuse risks, and he proposes narrow measures rather than broad AI regulation.

members.name: Roger F. Wicker

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as having 'nearly unlimited potential to benefit humanity' and as central to economic and military leadership. He mentions privacy, job and community concerns, but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says the nation that wins in AI will lead the 21st century and that AI is evolving very fast and is very important. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He frames China's AI advances as a direct national security threat. He never raises loss of control or existential risk, and his other concerns are everyday harms such as deepfakes, privacy, jobs and utility bills.
just.china_race: Winning the AI race against China is a recurring and dominant lens for him. He uses it to oppose the diffusion rule and to argue for a 'light touch' approach, though he also supports some protections.
just.regulation: He explicitly wants a 'light touch' for AI regulation and opposed the diffusion rule as burdensome. He backs narrow measures such as the Take It Down Act and data-center ratepayer standards.

members.summary: Wicker talks about AI mainly as a strategic and economic contest with China that the U.S. must win. He backs light-touch regulation and opposes burdensome export rules, but supports targeted measures on deepfakes and on data-center costs for ratepayers. He acknowledges privacy and job concerns but does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Susan M. Collins

just.ai_overall: She explicitly calls for balancing AI's promise (medical advances, accessibility) against its risks, and most of her other statements focus on specific harms like scams, election deception, cyber risk, and data center costs. This fits a mixed, balanced view.
just.agi_pilled: She talks about AI in several contexts but only as a rapidly evolving normal technology with specific harms. None of her statements mention AGI or economy-wide transformation.
just.x_risk: She flags cyber risk to AI systems and calls for protecting critical infrastructure, which is a national-security-scale concern. She never mentions loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. The only competitive framing is a brief reference to maintaining American leadership in AI innovation, so the race is a minor factor.
just.regulation: She backs targeted rules: election deepfake legislation, data center ratepayer protections and guardrails, and consumer protections. She also opposes a federal moratorium on state AI laws. She does not propose broad frontier-model frameworks, liability, or licensing.

members.summary: Collins talks about AI mainly in terms of concrete, practical issues: deceptive AI content in elections, scams, cyber risk to critical infrastructure, and data center electricity costs for Maine ratepayers. She says AI offers real promise, such as medical advances, but that it carries risks and Congress should act. She backs targeted legislation and opposes a federal moratorium on state AI laws, while saying little about AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: John Cornyn

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as a strategic and economic opportunity: 'world-changing technology,' the 'new space race,' and strong support for AI infrastructure. He does acknowledge harms to children, but treats broader fears as hype.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will shape national security, economic dominance and 'the future of the world,' which is transformative on the scale of a space race. He does not himself make AGI or superintelligence claims. The only AGI mention is a shared article, and he dismisses hype.
just.x_risk: He calls existential-risk talk 'hype' and 'scare tactics' and labels Harris's warning about humanity's existence 'scaremongering.' He also shares pieces dismissing AI doomers and overhyped risk.
just.china_race: Beating China in AI is a recurring, primary lens across his floor speeches and posts. He uses it to push outbound-investment limits and chip and data-center buildout, and to question whether regulation is wise. He still pairs it with child-safety concerns, so it does not fully override other priorities.
just.regulation: He backs narrow measures such as AI-generated CSAM penalties, the TAKE IT DOWN Act and the GUARD Act. He is skeptical of broad AI regulation, asking why not regulate sectors instead and whether Congress can keep up or adversaries will follow the rules.

members.summary: Cornyn talks about AI mainly as a strategic competition with China and an economic and infrastructure opportunity, especially for Texas data centers, chips and energy. He is skeptical of existential-risk 'hype' and of broad AI regulation, but sponsors targeted bills on AI-generated child sexual abuse material and chatbot harms to children. Much of his feed is shared articles, so many of his views are inferred from his own floor remarks and commentary.

members.name: Richard J. Durbin

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges promise ("great promise," "incredible potential," "lean into the AI revolution"), but most of what he says focuses on harms such as deepfakes, chatbot harms to teens, copyright violations, and Big Tech's lack of accountability. Harms dominate his framing, though he does not treat AI as purely a threat.
just.agi_pilled: He asks whether AI is a qualitative change and a "game changer," compares it to the transformation brought by phones, and says it will "profoundly transform the American workplace." He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: deepfakes, misinformation, cybercrime, job upheaval, chatbot harms to kids, copyright, and grid costs. He does not frame any risk as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: China appears only once, in a remark about its surveillance use of AI. He also criticizes the "arms race" argument for being used to sidestep creators' rights, so race framing is minimal and he is skeptical of it.
just.regulation: He consistently calls for substantial regulation, including a federal cause of action and developer liability (the AI LEAD Act), and opposes preemption of state AI laws. He also backs the targeted DEFIANCE Act. His stated aim is comprehensive AI legislation, though he does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Durbin speaks about AI mainly through the lens of harms and accountability, especially nonconsensual deepfakes, chatbot harms to children, and copyright. He acknowledges AI's promise but repeatedly says Congress must regulate it, and he opposes federal preemption of state AI laws. He sponsors liability and victim-lawsuit bills (the AI LEAD Act and the DEFIANCE Act) and rarely raises China or existential risk.

members.name: Mitch McConnell

just.ai_overall: He welcomes AI infrastructure in Kentucky and acknowledges 'valid concerns' about deepfakes, but he never gives an overall view of AI's promise versus its risks.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformative effect. He calls AI an 'emerging and important technology' and lists it among other war technologies.
just.x_risk: The only risk he raises is deepfakes in political speech. He says nothing about catastrophic or existential risk, and he doesn't reject it either.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. 'Greater U.S. leadership in AI' is only a faint hint of competition, which is too thin to score.
just.regulation: He is wary of acting hastily on deepfake rules, noting Congress hasn't even defined AI and that 'leading with our chin' is unwise. He also asks what role government should play at all. This points to a cautious, light-touch stance.

members.summary: McConnell talks about AI sparingly and mostly in practical terms: he welcomes AI infrastructure in Kentucky as a national security and economic win, and he lists AI among the technologies changing warfare while stressing the importance of munitions stockpiles. On regulation, he is cautious. He grants that deepfake concerns are valid but warns Congress against moving before it understands what it is regulating.

members.name: Jeff Merkley

just.ai_overall: He says he wants to reap AI's benefits, but nearly all of his statements stress harms: election disinformation, discrimination, and voter suppression. The harms clearly dominate, with only a brief nod to benefits.
just.agi_pilled: He notes that AI is changing 'so fast' and that even experts don't understand it. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation.
just.x_risk: His strongest catastrophic concern is that AI should not launch nuclear weapons, which is a national-security catastrophe scenario. He also speaks of safety of new models and of AI in the wrong hands, but he never discusses loss of control or extinction.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned. His comments on AI chips to the UAE concern corruption, not competition.
just.regulation: He backs an FDA-like agency to vet new AI models. He also authored the 'most comprehensive' AI Civil Rights Act and opposes the 10-year state-law moratorium.

members.summary: Merkley talks about AI mostly as a risk to democracy and civil rights, especially election disinformation, voter suppression, and bias. He says he wants AI's benefits, but his focus is on legislating: the FAIR Elections Act, the AI Civil Rights Act, a ban on autonomous AI nuclear launch, and an FDA-style agency for new models. He opposes the preemption of state AI laws and criticizes AI chip deals with the UAE as corrupt.

members.name: Jack Reed

just.ai_overall: He calls AI a powerful tool with real opportunities and real risks, and backs both responsible adoption (the Bryant AI hub, the military AI budget) and guardrails. Concern about misuse, corporate overreach and price discrimination is prominent, but he does not treat AI as mainly a threat.
just.agi_pilled: He treats AI as a powerful, fast-evolving technology with specific harms and uses (pricing, scams, military deployment). Nothing in his statements mentions AGI, superintelligence or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: He worries about misuse by bad actors, unsafe rushing of AI, and AI in military operations. In a floor speech he cites warnings that AI could destroy the species, framing the military domain as where that would show up first, but he never explicitly discusses loss of control.
just.china_race: China appears repeatedly: he criticizes chip sales to China as a national security failure and notes PRC AI threats. He also rejects the idea that guardrails mean losing to China, so the race is a recurring but balanced theme.
just.regulation: He repeatedly calls for congressional oversight, standards and governance, and he backed a federal oversight framework for frontier AI models. He opposes preempting state AI laws and wants AI firms to bear their costs, though he stops short of calling for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Reed describes AI as a powerful technology with both opportunities and risks, and says Congress must provide balanced oversight, standards and guardrails. He opposes federal preemption of state AI laws, criticizes the Trump administration's rejection of guardrails, and focuses on consumer harms such as surveillance pricing and scams, plus military AI deployment. He supports responsible AI adoption and treats China as a real competitor, but argues that guardrails need not mean falling behind it.

members.name: James E. Risch

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as transformational and revolutionary, and uses it in nuclear and energy work. He also flags misuse by malicious actors and adversaries, but he frames these risks as manageable through standards and safeguards.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will 'transform the way we live, do business' and calls it a 'transformational technology' that will shape the future. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He warns of AI-powered cyberattacks, information operations, and adversary battlefield systems, which are national-security-scale risks. He also supports human control over nuclear weapons decisions, but he does not frame loss of control of advanced AI as a general concern.
just.china_race: China is a recurring adversary in his AI remarks. He stresses that the U.S. must lead, protect sensitive technologies from China, tighten export controls, and secure 'American dominance.' The framing is balanced somewhat by his support for guardrails and allied standards.
just.regulation: He supports targeted measures such as the TEST AI Act, guardrails, standards, and export controls, and he anticipates legislative action. He does not call for broad licensing or a new agency, and he stresses continued innovation leadership.

members.summary: Risch talks about AI mainly through national security, foreign policy, and energy. He calls it transformational and wants the U.S. and its allies to lead, set standards, and block China and other adversaries from stealing or exploiting the technology. He backs targeted guardrails, testing, and export controls rather than broad regulation, and he does not discuss AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Jeanne Shaheen

just.ai_overall: She says AI holds 'extraordinary potential for both promise and peril' and says it needs to be harnessed while its risks are mitigated. Her statements cover election deepfakes, jobs and kids' safety, along with innovation and competitiveness.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or transformative change at the scale of an industrial revolution. Her remarks are about specific harms and about technology competitiveness.
just.x_risk: She cites 'the threat uncontrolled AI poses' and says AI deepfakes and disinformation are among the gravest threats to the U.S. This is serious national-security and election-integrity concern. Her one mention of 'uncontrolled AI' is brief, so it is not a clear loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: She frames chip exports to China as squandering America's 'primary advantage in the AI race' and stresses competing on technology and protecting the U.S. competitive edge. China competition is a recurring lens, though she pairs it with safety and regulation concerns and does not use it to argue against rules.
just.regulation: She opposes the 10-year state-law moratorium and wants Congress to act on AI. She backs funding for NIST testing, evaluation and safety work and an AI Safety Institute, and she faults Congress for inaction. She also supports targeted rules on deepfakes and election robocalls, but her overall stance is substantively pro-regulation.

members.summary: Shaheen treats AI as having both promise and peril. She focuses most on election deepfakes and disinformation, kids' safety and jobs, and on keeping advanced chips away from China to preserve U.S. technological leadership. She criticizes congressional inaction and the proposed state-law moratorium, and she supports funding for AI safety testing at NIST. In one 2026 post she warned about 'uncontrolled AI.'

members.name: Mark R. Warner

just.ai_overall: He calls himself an "AI optimist" and a "pro-AI, pro-tech guy" who sees real upside. Most of his statements, though, stress serious risks to elections, jobs, kids and security, and he frames AI as "one of the greatest potential tools and risks."
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as "the biggest technological and economic disruption of our lifetimes" and one of the most consequential transformations in history, and he calls for a "radical transformation" of how workers are retrained. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: He warns of catastrophic harm ("AI could take down entire banks or local water systems") and says "human beings should be in charge of AI—not the other way around." He explicitly rejects an "imminent existential threat" while still affirming a "potentially catastrophic threat," so he is concerned about loss of control but does not make it a top priority.
just.china_race: China competition recurs in his statements: AI as a national security edge, criticism of chip sales to China, and opposition to a data center moratorium because "China is gonna move quicker." He balances this with safeguards and has said regulation can be added "and not lose the race."
just.regulation: He pushes substantial rules, including pre-testing of frontier models, an AI safety framework, fiduciary duties for AI agents, incident reporting and disclosure requirements, and he has tried to force a floor vote. He does not call for licensing or a new agency, and he says he wants to leave "room for innovation."

members.summary: Warner calls himself an AI optimist and a tech veteran, but nearly all of his statements stress risk and the need for guardrails. He focuses most on election deepfakes and misinformation, financial-market manipulation, job displacement (especially entry-level work), kids' safety and national security. He has introduced many bills and increasingly urges Congress to act now. He says AI could be catastrophic if mishandled but is not an imminent existential threat, and he treats China competition as one concern among several.

members.name: Kirsten E. Gillibrand

just.ai_overall: She mostly frames AI through harms: scams, deepfakes, healthcare denials, military use and surveillance. She does acknowledge benefits, such as helping seniors, curing disease, and AI innovation that helps everyone, but the harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She calls for AI aligned with humanity and says AI is developing rapidly. She never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation, so the statements don't show whether she expects transformative AI.
just.x_risk: She warns that deploying powerful military AI without guardrails could have 'catastrophic consequences'. She also pushes to keep humans in the loop on lethal decisions and nuclear weapons, which is a national-security catastrophe framing. She does not clearly discuss loss of control over advanced AI.
just.china_race: China appears as a secondary theme. She criticizes selling advanced chips to China and says the administration's policy pushes the world toward Chinese alternatives and threatens competitiveness. She pairs this with safety and rules rather than making the race her main lens.
just.regulation: She repeatedly calls for clear rules of the road, safety guardrails and oversight, and a framework for AI companies. She has introduced legislation on military AI and on AI in Medicare claims. This goes beyond narrow targeted fixes, though she stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Gillibrand talks about AI mainly as a source of harm to seniors, children and voters, through scams, deepfakes, healthcare claim denials and surveillance. She also raises military uses, insisting humans stay in control of lethal decisions. She says she backs innovation and notes benefits like medical breakthroughs, and she argues for clear federal rules and guardrails. She sometimes frames this as a matter of competitiveness with China, and she often criticizes the Trump administration's AI policy.

members.name: Christopher A. Coons

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs AI's promise (creativity, healthcare, innovation) with serious harms, and by late 2026 he calls AI an existential threat. The balance is real promise alongside real risk, which fits mixed/balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI could radically reshape society, may define the rest of the century, and is advancing in ways designers can't predict or fully control. He never explicitly mentions AGI or superintelligence, so this stops at very transformative.
just.x_risk: He calls AI an existential threat that should top the Trump–Xi agenda, and cites Cold War nuclear arms control as a model to avoid destroying humanity. He also endorses Amodei's warning about models that can't be fully controlled. Much of his earlier record covers ordinary harms, but his recent framing treats existential risk as a top priority.
just.china_race: Competition with China is a recurring, primary lens, especially on chip export controls and 'winning the AI race'. He also calls for US–China guardrails and says the race is 'off a cliff', so it does not override his other concerns.
just.regulation: He backs substantial rules: independent oversight of AI models, transparency and safety guardrails for AI companies, whistleblower protections, and guardrails to slow AI development. He also champions many targeted bills (NO FAKES, election deepfakes), but his stance goes beyond targeted rules without calling for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Coons describes AI as having large potential benefits but needing guardrails. Most of his statements are about bipartisan bills on deepfakes and likeness (NO FAKES), election deception, and transparency. He frames chip export controls around beating China in AI. By late 2026 he calls AI an existential threat, urges US–China talks on guardrails, and says Congress must act since the White House won't.

members.name: Robert B. Aderholt

just.ai_overall: The statements treat AI as a strategic priority for research investment and military dominance, but they never state an overall feeling about AI's promise versus its harms. Interest in funding and advancing AI is not enough to place a score.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation. They discuss AI only as a research and warfighting domain.
just.x_risk: There is no discussion of catastrophic or existential risk. The only nod to downsides is a passing reference to 'ethical, legal, and societal implications' in a summary of the federal plan.
just.china_race: China is never named, and the call for 'domination' of warfighting domains including AI hints at competition but doesn't explicitly frame an AI race with China.
just.regulation: The statements concern research investment, public-private partnerships, and budget priorities. They take no position on regulating AI.

members.summary: Aderholt talks about AI mainly as a strategic and budgetary matter. He asks the administration how it will carry out the national AI R&D plan and calls for U.S. dominance in warfighting domains including AI. The statements don't address regulation, catastrophic risk, AGI, or China directly.

members.name: Tammy Baldwin

just.ai_overall: She cites real promise (productivity, research, weather forecasting, safety) alongside serious concerns about corporate power, worker displacement, chatbot harms, and loss of control. Neither side clearly dominates, and her recent statements lean more toward the risks.
just.agi_pilled: She mentions AI operating beyond human control and 'frontier models', but never discusses AGI, superintelligence, or timelines. Her statements about AI reshaping workplaces don't establish an expectation of transformative change on their own.
just.x_risk: She says she hears the public's concern that AI might operate beyond human control. She calls for independent testing so models can be 'kept under human control' and for a halt to deployment otherwise, which treats loss of control as a real concern. She does not frame it as extinction or a top-tier priority comparable to nuclear war.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race. The one reference to American-made AI concerns research funding, not geopolitical competition.
just.regulation: She calls for an independent regulator with authority to block deployment of frontier models until testing shows they are safe, plus mandatory disclosure of risks and incidents. She also stresses oversight and guardrails, and says Big Tech cannot be trusted to police itself. This amounts to a pre-deployment approval regime and a new oversight body.

members.summary: Baldwin describes AI as a technology with real benefits for research, health, weather forecasting, and productivity, but her recent statements focus on risks and corporate power. She stresses protecting workers, patients, and families from harms such as algorithmic care decisions, deepfakes, chatbot harms, and data center costs. She also calls for an independent regulator able to halt frontier model deployment and for ensuring AI stays under human control.

members.name: Michael F. Bennet

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs acknowledgment of AI's transformative potential (drugs, diagnostics, climate, economy) with strong emphasis on harms to kids, democracy and privacy. Harms get most of the airtime, but he consistently frames AI as real promise plus real risk, which fits mixed/balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as a technology able to 'profoundly transform our economy and society' and calls this a 'world-altering moment', comparable to past industrial regulatory challenges. He never explicitly mentions AGI or superintelligence, though he cites company estimates of humanity being destroyed.
just.x_risk: He cites industry leaders warning of risks to humanity on par with pandemics and nuclear war, and says to take seriously a 10-20% chance AI destroys humanity. He calls the stakes 'existential' and wants the power to pause unsafe AI. His main emphasis remains everyday harms, so this stops short of making it a top-tier priority.
just.china_race: China competition is a recurring but secondary theme: he backs an Office of Global Competition Analysis, opposes chip sales to China, and wants AI regulation that keeps America competitive. He does not use the race to argue against regulation, and the bulk of his AI talk is about domestic safeguards.
just.regulation: He has repeatedly championed a new independent federal agency to regulate AI and Big Tech (the Digital Platform Commission). He backs pre-release assessment of powerful models, the power to pause unsafe technology, and penalties of up to 15% of global revenue. He rejects voluntary commitments as insufficient.

members.summary: Bennet presents AI as a technology with real transformative promise but spends most of his attention on harms to children, elections, privacy and democracy. He has made a new independent federal regulator for AI and Big Tech his signature proposal and says voluntary industry commitments and the Trump administration's approach are inadequate. He also cites warnings from AI executives about existential risk and backs limits on AI chip exports to China, but China and AGI are secondary themes.

members.name: Gus M. Bilirakis

just.ai_overall: He mostly describes AI as a major opportunity for the economy, healthcare, manufacturing and security, and he treats harms such as scams, deepfakes and chatbot harms to kids as manageable through targeted measures. He does acknowledge real risks, but the optimism dominates.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'transformative technology' that can 'transform our economy' and reshape the global economy. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns are everyday harms: scams, deepfakes, child exploitation, chatbot suicides, privacy and IP scraping. He says AI 'can be weaponized' only in passing and mentions no catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.
just.china_race: He repeatedly describes a global race and warns of ceding AI leadership to China. He uses the race to argue against heavy-handed regulation, but he still pairs it with consumer protection, so it falls short of dominant.
just.regulation: He backs narrow measures such as Take It Down, the KIDS Act and the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. He warns against burdensome rules, says existing laws already cover AI, and criticizes the EU AI Act and 'conflicting' AI legislation. That adds up to a light-touch, pro-innovation position.

members.summary: Bilirakis speaks about AI mostly as an economic and competitive opportunity in manufacturing, healthcare, energy demand and cybersecurity. He frames AI policy around keeping U.S. leadership ahead of China and criticizes the EU's heavy regulation. He supports targeted measures against scams, deepfakes, harms to kids and content scraping, but cautions Congress against imposing broad new obligations on AI developers.

members.name: Sanford D. Bishop, Jr.

just.ai_overall: He promotes AI's agricultural and educational benefits, and he also acknowledges workforce, privacy, and community tradeoffs, notably around data centers. His tone is balanced rather than strongly positive or negative.
just.agi_pilled: He calls the AI moment 'unprecedented' in education, but he never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation on the scale of the internet.
just.x_risk: He mentions national security only in passing and never discusses catastrophic, misuse, or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race. He speaks only of staying 'on the cutting edge' in agriculture and education.
just.regulation: He says he will listen to constituents as Congress tackles AI policy and advises local officials and data center developers on tradeoffs and community assurances. He backs no specific federal AI regulation.

members.summary: Bishop mostly talks about AI as a practical tool, especially for agriculture and education, and has sponsored a bill to fund AI and mechanization research at land-grant universities. He also acknowledges concerns about workforce effects, privacy, and the local costs of data centers, such as energy, water, and utility rates. His statements are measured and local in focus, with little on AGI, catastrophic risk, China, or specific regulation.

members.name: Marsha Blackburn

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs enthusiasm for AI innovation (health care, nuclear energy, data centers, jobs) with sharp warnings about harms to kids, creators and conservatives. She calls AI "a powerful tool, but it also comes with risks," which reads as balanced.
just.agi_pilled: In a 2023 hearing she said superhuman AI is "not decades away" but "perhaps just a couple of years away." This is the only AGI-type statement, and most of her other remarks treat AI as an ordinary technology, so the evidence is thin.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: child safety, deepfakes, copyright, bias, fraud and privacy. She nods to preventing "catastrophic events" but says the doomsday discussion should not crowd out AI's benefits, and she never raises loss of control.
just.china_race: Beating China in the AI race recurs in her framing, including "America wins the AI race" and ruling out China from regulatory talks. She consistently pairs it with protections for kids and creators rather than using it to oppose rules.
just.regulation: She backs substantial federal rules: the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act as "one rulebook," KOSA's duty of care, NO FAKES, and legal accountability for harmful tools. She also wants federal preemption, but only after a real national standard exists, and she opposed the moratorium without one.

members.summary: Marsha Blackburn talks about AI mainly as a source of concrete harms: sexualized chatbots and toys for kids, deepfakes and voice cloning, uncompensated use of creators' work, and perceived bias against conservatives. She also promotes AI innovation in Tennessee and says the U.S. must beat China. She pushes for one federal rulebook, her TRUMP AMERICA AI Act, along with KOSA and NO FAKES, and she rarely discusses AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Richard Blumenthal

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges AI's 'immense promise' and says we should not have to choose between innovation and safeguards. But nearly all of his statements stress harms: kids, privacy, deepfakes, jobs, costs, and security threats, with Big Tech portrayed as untrustworthy.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as a 'new industrial revolution' and 'a new era' that is 'moving at accelerating speed.' He says AI is 'no longer science fiction,' but he never explicitly discusses AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He warns of 'catastrophic failure,' 'rogue' AI agents, and the need to 'monitor and control' increasingly sophisticated and dangerous models. He also stresses large-scale misuse such as cyberattacks. He never frames this as extinction-level or a top priority, so he lands at 3 rather than 4.
just.china_race: He accepts that winning the AI race is 'absolutely necessary' and cites Chinese hacking of Anthropic's tools. He uses China mainly to argue for more safeguards, not to argue against regulation, and it is not his primary lens.
just.regulation: He repeatedly calls for a licensing regime, a new independent oversight agency, and statutory pre-release safety evaluation. He also backs liability, criminal penalties, and opposes preemption of state laws.

members.summary: Blumenthal talks about AI mainly as a source of harm that needs enforceable rules. He focuses on children and chatbots, deepfakes, privacy, data-center energy costs, and security threats, and he often criticizes Big Tech and the White House for siding with industry. He pushes for a federal oversight agency, licensing, and independent evaluation of frontier models. He also nods to AI's promise and to the need to beat China, and he warns of catastrophic failures and 'rogue' AI.

members.name: John Boozman

just.ai_overall: He mostly describes AI as an opportunity, citing its potential in agriculture, road safety and assistive tech for people with autism. He also briefly says to 'ask tough questions about the potential risks,' so the optimism is not unqualified.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI 'has the incredible potential to affect nearly every aspect of our society' and refers to its 'transformative potential.' He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises are ordinary ones: consumer safety, sensitive data and agricultural cybersecurity. None are framed as catastrophic or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He worries that new AI rules for insurers would duplicate existing frameworks and hurt policyholders. He allows that 'new regulations may be needed' for consumer safety and data, but he is cautious and favors targeted rules at most.

members.summary: Boozman talks about AI mostly as a practical tool for agriculture, road safety and assistive technology, and he praises students' work with it. He sometimes notes risks such as consumer data and cybersecurity and says new rules may be needed, but he warns against regulatory duplication. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk or China.

members.name: Vern Buchanan

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as an opportunity for health care, fraud detection, manufacturing and American leadership, and wants it to thrive 'without unnecessary constraints.' He does acknowledge harms such as deepfakes and scams, but treats them as manageable with targeted fixes.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation on the scale of the internet or industrial revolution. His AI talk centers on specific applications and leadership.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns are everyday harms: deepfake exploitation of children, AI scams, and election robocalls. None involve catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: China competition appears repeatedly, as in the criticism of the AI Diffusion Rule for letting China get ahead and the push to keep America ahead of China. It sits alongside other themes such as fraud, health and child safety, and is not described as overriding everything else.
just.regulation: He backs targeted rules, including the TAKE IT DOWN Act, the AI Fraud Accountability Act and election protections. He also opposes 'unnecessary constraints,' criticizes the AI Diffusion Rule, and objects to MedPAC's approach to AI tools, so he does not favor broad frameworks.

members.summary: Buchanan speaks about AI mostly as an economic, health and government-efficiency opportunity, citing IRS fraud detection, health care applications, and American leadership. He supports narrow legislation on deepfake exploitation of children and AI-enabled scams, and he wants to avoid constraints that would slow innovation. He sometimes uses a China-competition framing, but he does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Ken Calvert

just.ai_overall: He frames AI as an area of US advantage and military value that should be kept ahead, while saying unintended consequences should be avoided. Risks are treated as manageable, so he leans optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation. AI is discussed only as a capability to lead in and to use in the military.
just.x_risk: He refers to vague 'unintended consequences' that industry figures have raised, with no catastrophic or existential framing and no dismissal of such risks. This is too thin to score.
just.china_race: He stresses maintaining the US lead and says China and other adversaries will not slow down. Competition is a primary lens, though he does not use it to argue explicitly against all constraints.
just.regulation: He says we should avoid unintended consequences and that 'the horse is out of the barn,' but proposes no specific rules or framework. His stance on regulation is unclear.

members.summary: Ken Calvert talks about AI mainly as a matter of US competitiveness and military strength. He wants America to keep its lead over China and other adversaries and notes that China will not slow its development. He mentions avoiding unintended consequences and local power and water strain from data centers, but gives no specific regulatory proposals.

members.name: Shelley Moore Capito

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly stresses AI's benefits (health, cures, education, defense, economy) and pairs them with caution about dangers, kids' safety, privacy, and fraud. The risks read as manageable, so the lean is optimistic rather than evenly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: She calls AI's pace unlike anything seen before, likening it to the early internet 'times 100,000 times faster,' and says it will carry the country for decades. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: Her stated concerns are everyday harms: children's safety, privacy, fraud, scams, deepfakes, and impacts on workplaces. She makes vague mentions of 'dangers' and 'detrimental effects' but never frames them as catastrophic or about loss of control.
just.china_race: She repeatedly frames AI as a race for international superiority, names competition with China, and justifies data centers by it. She says the U.S. can't slow down or it loses the race, though she also supports some safeguards.
just.regulation: She backs targeted measures such as the AI scam and deepfake prohibition, child and privacy safeguards, and voluntary guidelines (VET AI Act). She also says Congress will 'look at regulations' and welcomes an industry-requested 'regulatory floor,' but she proposes no broad framework.

members.summary: Capito talks about AI mostly as a major opportunity, especially for health care, defense, education, and West Virginia's economy, while saying safeguards are needed for children, privacy, and fraud. She often uses race language about beating China and building data centers and energy capacity to win. She supports targeted and voluntary measures and a bipartisan look at a regulatory floor, and she does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: André Carson

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as a powerful tool that can do a great deal of good, and he also stresses job loss, surveillance, rogue agents, and the lack of guardrails. The promise and the risk are roughly balanced, and the tone leans toward urgency about safeguards.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI can have staggering impacts on public health, the economy, and communities, and that it is growing faster than we can keep up with. He mentions the 'global race toward Artificial Super Intelligence' only in passing, while describing a hearing, and does not give his own AGI expectations.
just.x_risk: He flags cybersecurity threats, surveillance, military use of AI, and the 'risk of rogue AI agents'. He wants a human making high-stakes decisions rather than a machine. This points to serious misuse and some loss-of-control concern, but he does not frame it as existential.
just.china_race: Beating China is a main lens in his AI statements: he says the stakes are 'could not be higher' and that Chinese AI models winning means censorship and surveillance. He pairs this with worker, civil rights, and utility-cost protections, and does not use the race to argue against regulation.
just.regulation: He says AI 'needs to be regulated' and urges action now. He backs the AI Civil Rights Act and a nationwide pause on new AI data centers until safeguards exist, and he sponsors transparency bills. The pause and the broad call for regulation put him at the strongly pro end.

members.summary: Carson describes AI as a powerful tool with real benefits that needs urgent safeguards. He often frames AI policy as a contest with China that the US must win with American values, and he also stresses protections for workers, civil rights, and utility costs. He strongly backs regulation, including a pause on new AI data centers, the AI Civil Rights Act, and military AI transparency and human-judgment requirements.

members.name: Bill Cassidy

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly stresses AI's benefits, especially in health care, cancer research and government efficiency, and treats job disruption as manageable. He also flags real risks to kids, privacy and control of superintelligence, so this is optimism with caveats.
just.agi_pilled: In a series of posts he treats superintelligence as a real possibility that requires planning, asking who governs whom if its judgments exceed human ability to evaluate them. He does not give explicit short timelines, so this stops short of 4.
just.x_risk: He argues that autonomous superintelligence could escape meaningful human control, and that AI could cause catastrophic harm through the digital systems civilization depends on. He discusses alignment, kill switches and loss of control at length, but does not compare AI to nuclear war or pandemics as a top priority.
just.china_race: He mentions China as a security threat (DeepSeek) and engages with the 'race to superintelligence' framing, but he criticizes that framing as a rationale for building something ungovernable. China is a recurring but secondary theme, balanced against other concerns.
just.regulation: He wants targeted rules on privacy, kids' safety, liability and worker safeguards, and he sponsors bills like COPPA 2.0 and the Health Information Privacy Reform Act. He opposes sweeping one-size-fits-all regulation. He also proposes limits on autonomy and recursive self-improvement, which pulls slightly toward more regulation, but the overall stance is targeted.

members.summary: Cassidy mostly talks about AI as a promising tool, especially for health care, veterans' benefits and government efficiency, while calling for protections for kids, privacy and workers. He opposes broad one-size-fits-all regulation and prefers targeted, context-specific rules. In late 2026 posts he turns to superintelligence, arguing that autonomous AI could slip out of human control and that humans must retain intention and authority. He rejects the framing that the US must win a race to build it.

members.name: Kathy Castor

just.ai_overall: Her statements focus almost entirely on harms: kids and chatbots, rent-setting algorithms, privacy, and data-center energy costs. She acknowledges AI's role in the economy and in grid tools, but the harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or radical transformation. She treats AI as a set of products and policy problems, which is not enough to place her on this scale.
just.x_risk: Her risk concerns are everyday harms: kids and chatbots, privacy, algorithmic rent-setting, and electricity costs. None of them has a catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: She invokes competition with China in a few places, saying tariffs are 'a gift to China' and that the AI race needs a modern energy policy. It is a recurring but secondary lens next to consumer protection.
just.regulation: She strongly opposes the moratorium on state AI laws and demands federal guardrails and a national framework. She supports transparency, kids' protections, comprehensive privacy rules with limits on AI-enabled decisions, and data-center cost rules. Her proposals are substantial but not licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Castor talks about AI mainly as a consumer-protection and cost-of-living issue. She stresses harms to kids from chatbots, algorithmic rent-setting, privacy, and the electricity costs of data centers. She sharply criticizes the push for a moratorium on state AI laws and calls for federal guardrails and privacy legislation. She also mentions the China race and AI-related energy needs, but not AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Judy Chu

just.ai_overall: Her statements about AI focus almost entirely on harms, namely wrongful care denials in Medicare Advantage, and she calls the technology 'scary.' She names no real benefits, though the concern is confined to one domain, so this is mostly concerned rather than very concerned.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation. They only cover AI use in health insurance coverage decisions and artists' work.
just.x_risk: She discusses only everyday harms such as wrongful denials of care and inaccurate algorithms. None of her statements frames AI risk as catastrophic or existential.
just.china_race: China and the AI race never come up in any of the statements.
just.regulation: She backs targeted oversight of AI in Medicare Advantage, including CMS monitoring, guardrails, and a prohibition on AI in coverage denials until the tools are verified. She does not propose a broad framework for AI generally.

members.summary: Judy Chu talks about AI almost entirely in the context of Medicare Advantage, where she says algorithmic tools wrongly deny seniors care. She has co-led bipartisan, bicameral letters urging CMS to step up oversight and to prohibit AI in coverage denials until the tools are shown to be reliable. She also briefly mentions protecting artists' work in the age of AI. Her statements do not address AGI, China, or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Yvette D. Clarke

just.ai_overall: She sometimes acknowledges AI's promise (for example "power and promise," "potential to improve the quality of life"), but nearly all of her statements stress harms such as deepfakes, bias, scams and loss of control. Benefits are mentioned briefly and the harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She talks about AI often and says it is advancing rapidly, but she frames it as a tool with specific harms. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence, and she says AI "always will be a tool in the toolkit."
just.x_risk: In 2026 she warns that frontier models have "broke containment" and exceeded the limits their creators assumed. She says humans must stay in the loop and that developers must prove they control their systems, which treats loss of control as a real concern. She does not frame it as extinction risk or a top-tier priority, and most of her other concerns are everyday harms.
just.china_race: China appears only occasionally: a national-security worry about China's AI plan, a mention of adversaries "not waiting" when she opposes the moratorium, and a claim that transparency is the path to leading the AI race. Race framing is not a main lens, and she does not use it to argue against regulation.
just.regulation: She backs substantial rules: the Algorithmic Accountability Act (impact assessments and audits), the AI Civil Rights Act mandates, and the DEEPFAKES Accountability Act, along with a strong federal framework, accountability for AI companies, and safety testing. She opposes the state-law moratorium and welcomes ending "unrestrained, unregulated AI." She does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Clarke frames AI mainly through harms: deepfakes and election disinformation, algorithmic bias and civil rights, scams, and Big Tech's lack of accountability. She has sponsored several bills (REAL Political Ads Act, DEEPFAKES Accountability Act, Algorithmic Accountability Act, AI Civil Rights Act) and strongly opposes federal preemption of state AI laws. In 2026 her focus widened to frontier-model safety incidents and loss of control. She treats AI as a powerful tool rather than a path to AGI, and she mentions China only occasionally.

members.name: Emanuel Cleaver

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges some potential (efficiency, innovation, workforce opportunity), but most of his statements stress harms: discrimination, job loss, deepfakes, threats to artists, and the line 'I reject any attempt to convince me that I should not be paranoid about AI.' Concern grows over time ('more concerned today than yesterday').
just.agi_pilled: He talks about rapid economic consequences from AI adoption and the need to prepare the workforce, which suggests broad transformation without naming AGI. His pop-culture references (Terminator, Matrix) and the remark about powerful systems dominating human decisions are not a clear AGI expectation.
just.x_risk: He endorses the concern that, without intentional rulemaking, powerful AI systems could dominate human decision making, and he cites the Terminator and Matrix as warnings. He also cites industry leaders on AI's potential for extraordinary damage to society. This signals loss-of-control concern, though he does not make it a top priority.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. Competitiveness appears only in passing, such as US competitiveness in AI and leadership in tech, and the UAE chips remark is a corruption critique. The race is not a framing for him.
just.regulation: He repeatedly demands congressional action and accountability. He criticizes Republicans for doing nothing to regulate AI, backs the Biden executive order on AI safety standards, and wants Congress to act on AI deepfakes. He has not specified licensing or a comprehensive framework, though.

members.summary: Cleaver speaks about AI mostly through its risks: bias and discrimination, fair housing, job and wage losses, nonconsensual deepfakes, and threats to artists. He also acknowledges some promise for efficiency and innovation, and he has backed workforce-preparation legislation and local AI funding. He calls for congressional action and accountability for tech companies, and once voiced concern that powerful AI could come to dominate human decision making.

members.name: James E. Clyburn

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as a threat, citing 'the very serious threat AI poses', 'unchecked artificial intelligence', deepfake disinformation, higher electricity bills and job insecurity. He names almost no benefits, so harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He repeats the claim that AI company leaders fear 'superintelligence' could cause catastrophic harm and criticizes Trump for encouraging it. He treats superintelligence as a real prospect worth planning for, though he gives no timelines and much of this is critique of Trump.
just.x_risk: He cites AI leaders' fears that superintelligence could cause catastrophic harm and says Trump is gambling with national security and public safety. He compares ignoring AI warnings to Covid-19. This treats catastrophic risk as real, but he doesn't put it at the top of his priorities or discuss loss of control directly.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He says 'we've got to put in place guardrails'. He repeatedly attacks Trump and others for rejecting AI regulation and safeguards, and he faults the push to block regulation. He supports substantial safeguards, but he proposes no specific framework such as licensing or liability.

members.summary: Clyburn talks about AI almost entirely as a threat, mostly in sharp criticism of President Trump. He accuses Trump of dismissing AI concerns, blocking regulation to protect the stock market and big tech donors, and encouraging superintelligence despite warnings of catastrophic harm. He also raises deepfake election disinformation, data-center electricity costs and job security, and he supports 'guardrails' without detailing specific policies.

members.name: Steve Cohen

just.ai_overall: Cohen welcomed xAI's arrival and acknowledges the "transformative economic potential" of data centers. He also repeatedly stresses environmental, energy-cost and community harms, and criticizes Musk's Grok. His view is mixed, and his concerns are mostly about infrastructure and specific harms.
just.agi_pilled: He never mentions AGI, superintelligence or human-level AI. "Transformative economic potential" refers to data centers, and the rest of his remarks are about energy, water and specific harms.
just.x_risk: His concerns are environmental, energy costs, and the reliability of Grok. He does not discuss catastrophic, existential or loss-of-control risk. Describing Grok's behavior as "not AI gone rogue" does not address x-risk.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an international AI race.
just.regulation: He introduced the Clean Cloud Act to put clean-energy standards and penalties on AI data centers and crypto miners. He has also pressed the EPA on xAI's turbines and demanded transparency. This is substantial regulation of AI infrastructure, but it is narrower than a frontier-model framework.

members.summary: Cohen talks about AI mainly through its local effects in Memphis, where xAI's supercomputer is located. He initially welcomed it for jobs and economic momentum, then became critical over water use, electricity demand, gas turbines and utility bills. He backs regulation of AI data centers through the Clean Cloud Act and criticizes Elon Musk and Grok, but does not discuss AGI, existential risk or China.

members.name: Tom Cole

just.ai_overall: He frames AI as an opportunity that drives advancement and as a tool for countering cyber threats. He voices no concerns about AI itself, though only two brief statements exist.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformative effects. Talk of 'next-generation advancement' is too vague to score.
just.x_risk: He does not discuss AI risks at all. The cyber threat he mentions comes from adversaries, not from AI itself.
just.china_race: He wants the U.S. to lead and be 'unrivaled' in AI, which is competitive framing. He also names China among several adversaries in cyber, but China is not explicitly the AI rival, and the framing is thin.
just.regulation: Neither statement takes a position on regulating AI. Both concern investment and U.S. leadership.

members.summary: Tom Cole speaks about AI briefly and positively. He presents it as a way to strengthen cybersecurity and to keep the U.S. at the front of technology. The statements contain no discussion of AI risks, AGI, or regulation.

members.name: Jim Costa

just.ai_overall: He praises AI's economic and agricultural potential (supercomputing, data-center opportunities) while raising concerns about data-center energy and water costs, election threats, and chip-export security risks. The balance is roughly even.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or AI on the scale of an industrial revolution. He talks about AI only in terms of specific applications and infrastructure.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises are everyday ones: election misinformation, utility costs, and resource strain. The chip-export national security remark is vague and not framed as catastrophic or loss of control.
just.china_race: The only link is a vague 'national security risks tied to advanced AI chip exports' and it does not name China or frame an AI race. Competition appears only in passing, as rural areas being able to compete.
just.regulation: He backs targeted measures: studies of data-center impacts, 'firewalls' on energy and water use, and federal legislation to slow data-center expansion. He also pushes for election security oversight. These are specific rules, not a broad framework.

members.summary: Costa describes AI as an economic opportunity, especially for agriculture and rural communities, and funded an AI supercomputing center in the Central Valley. His main concern is the strain AI data centers put on energy, water, and consumer utility bills, and he has sponsored bipartisan legislation to study these impacts and supports federal action to slow the buildout. He has also raised AI-driven election misinformation and chip-export security, but he does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Joe Courtney

just.ai_overall: He frames AI almost entirely through harms (child exploitation, deepfakes, rogue agents, a 'clear social cost') and mentions no benefits. He calls for industry accountability and safeguards, so he is mostly concerned rather than purely alarmist.
just.agi_pilled: He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation. Rogue agents and 'protect mankind' are about risk, not expected capability levels.
just.x_risk: He backs the AI Kill Switch Act to guard against rogue AI acting outside human control and says AI must 'remain under human control'. He also cites 'protect mankind', so loss of control is treated as a real concern, though he does not make extinction risk a top priority or compare it to nuclear war.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or a race with other countries.
just.regulation: He supports substantial rules: industry accountability, third-party emergency protections via the AI Kill Switch Act, deepfake criminalization, and urgent congressional action. He also cites AI CEOs calling for a slowdown. These go beyond narrow fixes, but he does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Courtney talks about AI mainly as a source of harm that Congress must address urgently. He cites child exploitation, non-consensual deepfakes and rogue AI agents. He backs bipartisan bills, including the AI Kill Switch Act and a deepfake criminalization bill, and criticizes the Speaker for recessing while AI executives warn of risks. He stresses keeping AI under human control and holding the industry accountable.

members.name: Mike Crapo

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as offering 'seemingly endless opportunities' and wants America to lead, while noting manageable concerns such as privacy, grid reliability and costs to ratepayers. This reads as mostly optimistic with some caution.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or transformation on the scale of the industrial revolution. His comments are about specific applications, health care, and infrastructure.
just.x_risk: He never discusses catastrophic, existential, or loss-of-control risks. The concerns he raises are privacy, grid reliability, and energy costs, but he does not address catastrophic risk either way.
just.china_race: He frames AI as a global race and says development must outpace China, and he says the U.S. must remain globally competitive. This sits alongside concerns about privacy, grid reliability and ratepayer costs, so it is present but balanced.
just.regulation: He is wary of legislating prematurely and warns that rigid, bureaucratic rules could stifle advances, so he prefers study and adaptability. He backs one targeted measure, making data centers pay for their own energy infrastructure.

members.summary: Crapo talks about AI as a large opportunity, especially in health care, and says America should lead and outpace China. He urges Congress to learn more before legislating and warns against rigid, one-size-fits-all rules. His most concrete policy stance is that data centers and other large-load customers, not ordinary ratepayers, should pay for the grid and infrastructure they need.

members.name: Eric A. "Rick" Crawford

just.ai_overall: He frames AI as a 'game changer' and a force multiplier, and he stresses the need to lead on it. He also admits unknowns ('we don't know what we're unleashing') and takes a balanced line on data centers, but opportunity and competition dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He says frontier labs 'may soon achieve self-improving AI' and that the U.S. must reach that threshold first. This treats transformative AI as a near-term possibility, but he does not use AGI language or give explicit timelines.
just.x_risk: His risk framing centers on national security, cyber, drones, and biothreats. He also says AI is 'the big unknown' and that 'we don't know what we're unleashing.' He never explicitly raises loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: The AI race with China is the main lens in most of his statements. He uses it to argue for export controls, more spending, and a dominance strategy, and he backs 'global dominance in AI.' He does balance this with some talk of responsible data center buildout.
just.regulation: He favors export controls, national-security evaluations, and faster AI adoption, with no support for broad domestic AI regulation. He supports government evaluation of frontier models by the NSA and wants a 'balanced approach' on data centers, but his focus is on competitiveness and spending rather than constraints on AI companies.

members.summary: Crawford discusses AI mostly through a national security and China-competition lens. He backs export controls, more spending, and faster adoption of AI in the intelligence community. He calls AI a game changer and notes that frontier labs may soon reach self-improving AI. He also says AI is a big unknown, but he rarely addresses domestic regulation or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Henry Cuellar

just.ai_overall: He mostly describes AI as an opportunity for education, trade logistics, defense, border security and government modernization. He pairs this with calls for responsible development and guardrails, and concerns about data-center costs and AI-generated abuse.
just.agi_pilled: He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or civilizational-scale change. His AI statements are about specific applications and funding, and calling AI "one of the defining challenges of our time" is too thin to score as transformative.
just.x_risk: He raises everyday harms such as deepfake abuse and data-center costs. He never discusses catastrophic, misuse-at-scale, or loss-of-control risks, and he does not dismiss them either.
just.china_race: One Spanish-language statement says the US can both set rules and win the race with China, which treats the race as real but compatible with regulation. It appears only once, so the theme is present but not dominant.
just.regulation: He says Congress must lead on AI regulation and calls for federal standards. He opposes stripping state authority, backs the Take It Down Act, supports oversight and guardrails, and proposes a bill of rights requiring data centers to pay their own costs. This goes beyond narrow fixes but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Henry Cuellar mostly talks about AI as an opportunity for his district, citing education grants, port logistics, border inspection technology, defense and government modernization. He also calls for responsible development, guardrails, and federal standards that do not preempt the states. He backs the Take It Down Act on deepfake abuse, wants data centers to cover their own water and electricity costs, and says the US can regulate and still beat China.

members.name: Diana DeGette

just.ai_overall: She says AI is here and raises concerns about cybersecurity, privacy, and scams, but also frames it as something to proceed with caution on rather than reject. Her statements are cautious but not clearly dominated by either promise or harm.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation from AI.
just.x_risk: She flags cyberattacks on the energy grid as a national security concern from AI reliance, which is a large-scale misuse risk. She does not mention loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned in the statements.
just.regulation: She calls for consumer guardrails, federal standards and disclosure for data centers, and privacy guardrails from Congress. She also questions a 10-year state AI moratorium. This points to substantial rules, though the proposals are mostly sector-specific.

members.summary: DeGette speaks about AI mostly through her energy and commerce work. Her concerns are grid cybersecurity, data center energy and water use, privacy, and voice-cloning scams. She favors guardrails, federal standards, and disclosure, and she questions a state-law moratorium. She also criticized one AI hearing as a distraction from public health issues.

members.name: Rosa L. DeLauro

just.ai_overall: Statements mention AI mostly as one sector among several in outbound-investment policy, or as a passing jab (AI image, 'their AI'). None gives a clear overall view of AI's promise or harm.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformative impact.
just.x_risk: No statement discusses catastrophic or existential AI risk. The national-security language concerns technology flowing to China, not AI risk itself.
just.china_race: China competition recurs in her statements: keeping AI, semiconductor, and quantum investment from funding China, and staying 'on the cutting edge' to stay ahead of China. It is framed together with worker and national-security concerns, not as a reason to oppose rules.
just.regulation: She voices support for AI oversight goals in a letter, but there are no details on domestic AI rules. Her focus is outbound investment screening, which is not AI regulation as such.

members.summary: DeLauro mostly mentions AI in the context of economic and national-security policy toward China, especially restricting U.S. outbound investment in AI, semiconductors, and quantum computing. She also expresses support for AI oversight goals in passing and uses AI references in political jabs. She says little about AI's broader benefits, risks, or future trajectory.

members.name: Scott DesJarlais

just.ai_overall: The statements only touch on AI in a defense and commercial-integration context. They do not express an overall view of AI's promise or risk.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or transformative change. One refers to 'the rise of AI and quantum computing in defense' without elaborating.
just.x_risk: Neither statement discusses AI risks of any kind, catastrophic or otherwise.
just.china_race: He links AI to staying ahead of adversaries (s1) and discusses China alongside AI and quantum computing in defense (s2). The framing is present, but the evidence is thin and not strongly developed.
just.regulation: Neither statement addresses AI regulation or rules.

members.summary: Scott DesJarlais discusses AI mainly through a defense and national-security lens. He praises commercial AI integration in military programs as a way to stay ahead of adversaries, and he mentions China, AI, and quantum computing in a radio interview. The statements do not address AI risks, regulation, or AGI.

members.name: Mario Diaz-Balart

just.ai_overall: He treats AI as inevitable and important, and wants to lead on it, but also wants controls so it does not 'get out of control.' The mix of promise and caution is balanced, though the evidence is thin.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements mention AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation from AI. They only describe AI as here to stay and as a defense technology.
just.x_risk: He wants verifiable controls so AI 'does not get out of control' and treats this as a matter for international agreements. That hints at a loss-of-control worry, but it is brief and not framed as catastrophic or existential, so it sits between everyday and serious concerns.
just.china_race: He says the US must stay on the cutting edge because China will not stop, and that unilateral restraint would not slow China. He also proposes verifiable agreements with China, which tempers the race framing, but competition is a primary lens.
just.regulation: He backs verifiable international agreements and says local communities should have a say, which is probably about data centers. He gives no clear position on domestic AI regulation.

members.summary: Diaz-Balart describes AI as inevitable and says the US must stay at the cutting edge because China will not stop. He favors a verifiable, 'distrust and verify' agreement with China to keep AI from getting out of control. He also encourages students in AI and technology, backs AI work at the Pentagon, and says local communities should have a say in projects imposed on them.

members.name: Lloyd Doggett

just.ai_overall: He praises AI uses in education, civic engagement and legal aid, and he also warns about AI in surveillance, autonomous weapons, insurance denials and bioweapons. Benefits and risks are roughly balanced, and most of his criticism targets the Trump administration's use of AI rather than the technology itself.
just.agi_pilled: He never discusses AGI, superintelligence or society-wide transformation. The only mention is a sarcastic reference to Trump's 'super intelligence' agreement, which does not show his own expectations.
just.x_risk: He warns that AI may enable a bioweapons race and infrastructure attacks, which counts as serious misuse. He does not raise loss of control, and his concern about machines making life-and-death decisions is about autonomous weapons rather than existential risk.
just.china_race: He mentions the global AI race, rivals and chip exports to China several times. He frames these around research funding and export controls, alongside other concerns, so the theme recurs without dominating.
just.regulation: He mocks voluntary company self-regulation, backs greater regulation and clear rules and accountability for military AI, and supports ethics guidelines and safeguards against mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. This is substantial pro-regulation sentiment, though he proposes no comprehensive framework such as licensing.

members.summary: Doggett talks about AI mostly through criticism of the Trump administration. He accuses it of weak self-regulation, lax chip export controls, retaliation against Anthropic, and reckless use of AI in surveillance, weapons, grant decisions and Medicare. He also promotes AI in education and student projects, calls for clear rules on military AI, and warns of bioweapon and infrastructure-attack risks, but he does not discuss AGI or loss of control.

members.name: Charles J. "Chuck" Fleischmann

just.ai_overall: He speaks about AI only in enthusiastic terms, as groundbreaking, 'the future,' and a driver of a 'New Golden Age' and national prosperity. He never mentions risks or harms.
