just.agi_pilled: She calls AI 'one of the biggest challenges of our time' and worries about powerful systems acting on their own and affecting jobs broadly. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence, so this fits transformative impact rather than AGI.
just.x_risk: She cites 'the total whole destruction of humanity' as a concern, worries about AI 'acting on its own,' and wants to slow the race to deploy powerful systems. Loss of control is treated as a real concern, though she does not make extinction risk her sole top priority.
just.china_race: She criticizes the international race to deploy powerful AI and calls for working with competitors and adversaries on shared safety standards. This rejects race framing in favor of cooperation.
just.regulation: She supports independent federal testing of powerful models before release, enforceable standards, audits, and whistleblower protections. She also wants development slowed and companies made to pay for disruption, which goes beyond targeted rules.

members.summary: Pingree speaks about AI mostly in terms of risk. She cites job loss, data-center environmental harm, AI acting autonomously, and even the possible destruction of humanity. She calls for slowing development, international safety coordination rather than a race, and strong federal testing and oversight of frontier models. She also criticizes Congress for deferring to tech companies and makes a pointed remark about AI's energy demands.

members.name: Mike Quigley

just.ai_overall: He says AI could bring enormous benefits (medical research, drug development) and also carries real risks, including loss of control. He pairs this with strong calls for oversight, which fits a balanced view.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI can kill more people than electricity or railroads and is advancing rapidly, which implies a transformative technology. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence, and his comparison to past technologies points to very transformative rather than AGI-level.
just.x_risk: He says humans could lose control of AI, citing AI CEOs, and backs a kill switch bill. He also says AI can kill more people than past technologies. He does not frame extinction as a top-tier priority, so a 3 fits better than a 4.
just.china_race: He rejects the 'winning the race with China' versus protecting-people framing as a false choice. He also calls for a standing AI dialogue with China to share safety incidents. He does not oppose competing, but the dialogue and the criticism of race framing fit the low end.
just.regulation: He wants Congress to stay in session until AI regulations are written, and he backs a kill switch bill, the FRONTIER Act with third-party auditors, independent inspectors, and a Select Committee on AI. He says AI should be regulated like airplanes and drugs and criticizes the administration's hands-off approach. This is broad, strongly pro-regulation.

members.summary: Quigley describes AI as a technology with major benefits, especially in medicine, and with serious risks, including loss of human control and potentially lethal harms. He strongly supports regulation, backing independent auditors, a kill switch, and a Select Committee on AI, and he criticizes the administration's hands-off approach. He rejects the idea that competing with China means skipping safeguards and proposes a US-China AI safety dialogue.

members.name: Harold Rogers

just.ai_overall: The only statement plausibly in his own voice (s1) notes ChatGPT and deepfakes and asks for AI education at DoD, which does not show an overall attitude. The "defining technology" and "go fast but keep a lid on risks" lines (s3) read like a Commerce Department witness's testimony, not his own.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI. Calling AI "the defining technology of our generation" (s3) is not clearly his and doesn't address AGI.
just.x_risk: No statement discusses catastrophic or existential AI risk. The only risks mentioned are deepfakes and AI ethics (s1) and generic "risks" (s3).
just.china_race: The China export-control statement (s2) is in the voice of the Commerce Secretary answering a question, not Rogers himself. Nothing else in the record ties him to a China framing.
just.regulation: Nothing here shows his position on AI regulation. He asks for DoD AI education (s1), and the other items are amendments by other members (s4) or funding requests apparently from a witness (s3).

members.summary: The record is thin and partly misattributed. Several quotes appear to come from other speakers, such as the Commerce Secretary testifying and members offering amendments. The one statement that seems to be his own asks the Defense Department to create an AI education program on concepts and ethics, citing ChatGPT and deepfakes. This is not enough to place him on any of the rubric's dimensions.

members.name: Mike Rogers

just.ai_overall: He calls AI "exciting" and "very pervasive," and backs AI R&D and workforce development. He raises only practical concerns, such as power needs and adversaries misusing the technology, so he leans optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will be "very pervasive in our society," comparing it to satellites, which suggests broad transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He worries about adversaries using AI maliciously, but he does not describe catastrophic, bioweapon, or loss-of-control scenarios.
just.china_race: He says rivals are outpacing the U.S. in AI and quantum computing, and he frames AI around adversaries and near-peers. Competition with China is a main lens, though he balances it with workforce and energy concerns.
just.regulation: He supports promoting AI R&D and a government directive, but he states no clear position on regulating AI companies or products.

members.summary: Rogers talks about AI mainly through national security, military modernization, and competition with adversaries. He presents it as exciting and pervasive, and he stresses workforce development, R&D, and the power and grid capacity it needs. He does not address catastrophic risk, AGI, or regulation of AI firms.

members.name: Steve Scalise

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as an opportunity and a driver of innovation and investment that should be harnessed. He acknowledges abuses and the need to protect consumers and kids, but treats these as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'revolution' and 'another advancement in technology,' which suggests significant change but nothing close to AGI. There is no mention of AGI or superintelligence, and the 'just another advancement' framing keeps him between ordinary tech and very transformative.
just.x_risk: The only risks he mentions are everyday ones: 'abuses,' consumer protection, and kids' online safety. He also says regulation is aimed at 'a problem that doesn't exist.' He does not frame anything as catastrophic and does not explicitly reject x-risk, so 1 fits better than 0.
just.china_race: Beating China is a dominant, recurring frame, and he uses it to argue against regulation and state laws. He says 'why would we want to cede ground' to China and describes a 'global race' for AI dominance that 'we cannot afford to lose.'
just.regulation: He opposes new heavy regulation and a new regulatory structure, and he backs a single federal set of rules over a state patchwork. He is open to addressing abuses and gaps and to kids' safety protections, which softens this slightly, but the emphasis is against constraints.

members.summary: Scalise talks about AI mostly as an engine of American innovation and investment. He repeatedly casts it as a race with China that the U.S. must win. He opposes heavy new regulation and state-level rules, favoring a single federal framework, while allowing for targeted action on abuses and kids' safety. He does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Janice D. Schakowsky

just.ai_overall: She occasionally acknowledges AI's transformative potential and says America should lead. Nearly all of her substantive statements stress harms such as scams, deepfakes, privacy erosion, deception and Big Tech abuse, so concerns dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is 'transforming our lives' and has 'transformative potential', which implies broad change. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence, so this stays at the lower 'transformative' level.
just.x_risk: Her risk concerns are everyday harms: fraud and voice cloning, deepfakes, privacy, kids' data, inequality, and jobs. None is framed as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: None of the statements addresses competition with China. 'America must be a leader in AI' is a general line and does not frame a race.
just.regulation: She strongly backs consumer guardrails, comprehensive federal privacy legislation as a base for AI regulation, accountability and transparency, and strong oversight of AI companies. She opposes preemption of state laws and a moratorium. Her proposals focus on consumer protection and are not licensing or a new agency, so she is pro-regulation but short of the top level.

members.summary: Schakowsky talks about AI mainly as a consumer-protection issue, focusing on scams, voice cloning, deceptive bots, deepfakes, data privacy and kids' safety. She acknowledges AI's transformative potential and says the US should lead, but her emphasis falls on holding Big Tech accountable. She strongly opposes federal preemption of state AI laws and calls for comprehensive privacy legislation and guardrails. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk or China.

members.name: Adam B. Schiff

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges AI's promise ("boundless opportunity," "potential to improve our lives"), but most of his statements stress harms: deepfakes, disinformation, rogue agents, risks to kids, job disruption, and existential threats. Harms dominate, though he does not treat AI as purely a menace.
just.agi_pilled: He speaks of "hurtling towards AGI and the unknown" and says frontier models are developing faster than experts thought possible. He also relays CEO warnings that AI could destroy humanity within a decade. He treats AGI as a real near-term possibility, though he does not give his own explicit timeline.
just.x_risk: He says he has heard about the "existential threat to humankind for years" and that frontier risks "could hold existential threats" and cause "catastrophic consequences." He also flags rogue AI agents and autonomous weapons. Loss of control is treated as a real concern, though he does not make it his single top priority.
just.china_race: He wants to confront China's efforts to overtake the U.S. in AI and to protect against foreign theft of AI advances. He pairs this with calls for safety coordination with China and with strong guardrails. It is a recurring but balanced theme.
just.regulation: He calls for mandatory industry-wide AI guardrails and for monitoring of frontier models rather than company self-policing. He also opposes federal preemption of state laws and backs many specific bills. This amounts to broad, strongly pro-regulation support.

members.summary: Schiff describes AI as a technology with real promise but frames it mostly through risks: election deepfakes, copyright and creator rights, kids and chatbots, military use, and worker disruption. In late 2026 statements he escalates to warnings about AGI, existential threats, and rogue AI agents. He consistently calls for mandatory guardrails, backs many specific bills, opposes preempting state laws, and wants safety coordination with China while also countering Chinese competition.

members.name: Charles E. Schumer

just.ai_overall: He pairs strong enthusiasm for AI's potential (curing disease, 'amazing potential', innovation as his 'North Star') with equally strong warnings about job loss, election harms and unchecked development. Neither side clearly dominates, so the view is balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI 'world-altering' and says it will 'reshape life on Earth'. He also names AGI as 'the ultimate goal' in the race with China and warns against encouraging superintelligence. This treats transformative AI and AGI as real, near-term possibilities, though he gives no explicit timelines.
just.x_risk: He repeatedly raises 'doomsday scenarios', the danger that we 'may prove incapable of managing this technology at all', bioweapons, and 'catastrophic risks from AI'. He held a forum on long-term risks and calls for classified briefings on them. Loss of control is treated as a real concern, though he does not compare it to nuclear war or pandemics.
just.china_race: Outcompeting China on AI and chips is a major, recurring lens for him. He says falling behind China on AI means 'we will fall behind everywhere' and attacks chip export loosening heavily. He still pairs the race with guardrails and does not use it to argue against regulation.
just.regulation: He says Congress 'must play a role in regulating AI' and pushes for substantial guardrails: a safety framework with model testing, the AI Safety Institute, transparency and election protections. He criticizes optional safety standards as not real guardrails. He does not call for licensing or a new agency, and he keeps stressing innovation.

members.summary: Schumer describes AI as both a historic opportunity and a serious danger, and he frames it as a 'SAFE Innovation' project: innovation as the 'North Star' alongside government guardrails. He led the bipartisan AI Insight Forums, backed deepfake and election-protection bills, and warns of job loss, bias and 'doomsday scenarios'. Later statements focus on attacking the Trump administration over AI chip sales to China and on demanding briefings about catastrophic AI risk, and he mentions AGI and superintelligence as stakes in the race with China.

members.name: David Schweikert

just.ai_overall: He calls himself a "huge AI optimist" and mostly presents AI as a tool for health care, fraud detection, and government efficiency. He also acknowledges risks from scams, deepfakes, and foreign influence, so he is not at the very optimistic end.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as a "revolution" in health care and a force that could change labor and the economy, which is transformative. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms such as scams, deepfakes, and foreign disinformation, plus some societal chaos. He mocks the idea that "AI is going to destroy the world" as a cable-TV view, and he makes no loss-of-control argument.
just.china_race: China appears only in passing, as one of several foreign actors (with Russia and Iran) weaponizing AI for disinformation. He does not frame AI policy as a race.
just.regulation: He mainly argues that old regulations block beneficial AI and wants to "legalize" it, such as AI prescribing. He supports some targeted anti-fraud measures, but the dominant theme is deregulation and light-touch rules.

members.summary: Schweikert talks about AI mostly as a practical tool for cutting deficits and fraud, auditing the Pentagon, and lowering health care costs, and he calls himself a "huge AI optimist." He repeatedly urges legalizing AI uses, such as AI prescribing, that he says outdated rules block. He also raises concerns about AI-enabled scams, deepfakes, and foreign influence operations, but not about existential risk or a race with China.

members.name: Austin Scott

just.ai_overall: His statements treat AI in passing, as a military tool or a broadband-dependent technology, and the data center remarks concern infrastructure, not AI itself. None of them states an overall view of AI's promise or harm.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or AI-driven transformation of society.
just.x_risk: He does not discuss catastrophic or existential AI risk. His only risk-related comments concern data center water and power use and the security of personal information.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned. He does say data centers should be located in the U.S. for national security and data protection, but that is not framed as competition with China.
just.regulation: He supports specific parameters for data centers on water use, cooling systems, and power costs, and says companies should pay their own energy costs. These are targeted infrastructure conditions, not broad AI regulation.

members.summary: Austin Scott rarely talks about AI directly. He mentions it as a tool in the F-35 program and as one of several technologies that depend on broadband. His recent comments focus on data centers: he wants limits on water and power use, wants companies to cover their own energy costs so local residents' bills don't rise, and wants facilities kept in the U.S. for national security and data privacy.

members.name: Robert C. "Bobby" Scott

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges some potential benefits, such as algorithmic tools reducing hiring bias, and the aim of ensuring AI 'takes us forward.' But almost all of his statements stress harms: discrimination, job displacement, child abuse material, and eroded civil rights.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or transformative change on a civilizational scale. He treats AI as a technology with specific harms. The 'crossroads' language in s5 is too vague to count as expecting radical transformation.
just.x_risk: His concerns are all everyday harms: bias, discrimination, job loss, privacy, child sexual abuse material, and chatbots. He gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He says Congress must take an active role and develop 'thoughtful regulations.' He also opposes preventing states from protecting people from AI harms, and he calls for safeguards on discrimination in hiring and in AI risk models. This is substantial regulatory support, though he proposes no specific frontier-model licensing or agency.

members.summary: Bobby Scott talks about AI mainly through civil rights, worker protection, and child safety. He grants that AI could help, for example by reducing hiring bias, but stresses that it is not neutral and can entrench discrimination and displace workers. He argues Congress should write balanced regulations and criticizes efforts to block state protections. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Tim Scott

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly frames AI as a powerful tool that can raise productivity, wages and opportunity, and says he is confident the risks can be handled responsibly. He does acknowledge real risks (kids, bias, energy costs), but they read as manageable rather than dominant.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a powerful tool and says it will affect productivity, markets and 'the future', but never mentions AGI, superintelligence or the scale of transformation. That is too little to place him between ordinary tech and very transformative.
just.x_risk: The risks he names are everyday ones: kids' safety, algorithmic bias, censorship, electricity and water costs, and job loss. None is framed as catastrophic or loss-of-control.
just.china_race: Beating China is a dominant, recurring frame ('who wins the future, China or America?'). He calls for an aggressive posture toward China and criticizes Democrats as 'pawns' of a China-run campaign, and he opposes rules that would hamper innovation or push it overseas.
just.regulation: He backs targeted measures such as the ASK Act for kids, protections against algorithmic bias, data centers paying their own way, and the BLADE Act. He also criticizes the broad SEC AI rule as stifling innovation and wants solutions that don't hamper innovation.

members.summary: Tim Scott describes AI as a powerful tool that brings opportunity and risk, and he stresses worker augmentation, productivity and wage gains. He frames AI heavily through competition with China, wants U.S. technology to dominate the global stack, and supports export and security measures. His regulatory interest is targeted, covering kids' safety, algorithmic bias, and data centers paying for their own power, and he opposes broad rules that might stifle innovation.

members.name: Terri A. Sewell

just.ai_overall: She cites real promise (health care, economy, education) and says she is not anti-AI, but she also stresses harms to communities, election misinformation, and bias. Promise and risk get roughly equal weight.
just.agi_pilled: She calls AI a 'technological revolution' and says it will 'revolutionize' health care and the economy, which implies large-scale transformation. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday and local: election disinformation, bias, environmental and economic burdens, privacy, and labor. She frames none of them as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: She wants America to lead in AI innovation, but China appears only in passing, as a conflict zone (South China Sea). It is not a lens for her AI policy.
just.regulation: She cosponsored and backs a moratorium on new AI data center construction until Congress enacts comprehensive safeguards, and she calls for federal guardrails. The moratorium is a substantial intervention, though it targets infrastructure and not frontier model safety.

members.summary: Sewell describes herself as pro-innovation and not anti-AI, and she cites benefits for health care, education, and the economy. Her focus is on community impacts, especially environmental and economic burdens on underserved communities from data centers, and she cosponsored the AI Data Center Moratorium Act. She has also raised concerns about AI-driven election misinformation and bias, and about integrating AI into national security with proper checks.

members.name: Brad Sherman

just.ai_overall: He grants that AI is a powerful tool with benefits, but nearly all of his statements stress existential danger, job loss, exploitation of creators, and 'unspeakably dangerous' systems. Harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He repeatedly discusses superintelligence, self-aware AI, and a 'successor species' as central concerns. He says such systems are 'rapidly emerging' and says AI may lead the century. He often frames the timeline as the second half of the century, but in 2026 he describes the danger as present.
just.x_risk: He calls the risk 'beyond the apocalypse,' 'existential,' and a threat of AI 'taking over the world.' He has introduced legislation on it, urges more funding, and cites 'Everyone Dies.' It is his signature priority.
just.china_race: He criticizes chip sales to China and says Chinese AI would be built without safeguards, so competition is a recurring theme. But he explicitly says the question should not be how to beat China and calls for working with all nations, which places him between the two framings.
just.regulation: He criticizes Trump's refusal to regulate AI or make international agreements. He backs legislation and major funding for safety monitoring, and calls for compensation and property rights for creators. This amounts to substantial rules and oversight, though he does not specifically call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Brad Sherman talks about AI mainly as a potential existential threat, especially the emergence of self-aware, ambitious superintelligent systems. He has pushed for years for research and legislation to monitor and prevent this. He also raises chip exports to China, job losses, creators' rights, and discrimination, and he criticizes the lack of regulation and safety funding. He prefers international cooperation to a race with China.

members.name: Michael K. Simpson

just.ai_overall: The statements welcome AI infrastructure investment and raise data center cost concerns, but neither gives an overall view of AI itself. Both are about infrastructure and energy costs, not AI's benefits or risks.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformation of society.
just.x_risk: No statement discusses catastrophic or existential AI risk. The only concern raised is energy costs from data centers.
just.china_race: He refers to a 'global AI race' and American leadership in AI, but China is never named and the mention is brief. This is too thin to place on the China-framing scale.
just.regulation: He supports state and local guardrails on data centers to keep energy costs from rising for families. That is a targeted rule, not a broad AI framework.

members.summary: Simpson's two statements both concern AI infrastructure. He celebrates a national-lab site being picked for AI projects and talks of American leadership in the 'global AI race.' He also backs state and local guardrails on data centers to protect families from higher energy costs. He says nothing about AGI, catastrophic risk, or broader AI regulation.

members.name: Adam Smith

just.ai_overall: He praises AI applications (student apps, a defense AI factory) while raising concerns about chatbots' mental health effects and AI use in Medicaid preauthorization. The mix is fairly balanced, though the evidence is thin.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI. He notes AI's rapid pace and effect on workforce needs but does not describe radical transformation.
just.x_risk: His concerns are ordinary harms such as chatbot mental health effects and misunderstanding of capabilities between nations. He does not frame these as catastrophic or as loss of control, and the miscalculation remark is only a mild security concern.
just.china_race: He wants Trump and Xi to discuss controlling AI together, which signals cooperation rather than race framing. He also stresses the risk of misunderstanding between rivals.
just.regulation: He supports specific targeted measures such as mental health guardrails for AI chatbots, and wants policymaking frameworks to keep pace with technology. He has not endorsed a broad framework.

members.summary: Adam Smith talks about AI mostly in practical terms: celebrating student app winners, welcoming defense-tech jobs, and noting its effect on workforce needs. He raises concerns about chatbot mental health effects, AI in Medicaid preauthorization, and miscalculation in military AI. He favors US-China dialogue on controlling AI and targeted guardrails over broad rules.

members.name: Adrian Smith

just.ai_overall: He calls AI's efficiencies "amazing" and urges that we celebrate them. He raises no concerns in this statement.
just.agi_pilled: The statement covers current efficiency gains only. It says nothing about AGI or society-wide transformation.
just.x_risk: He does not mention catastrophic or existential risk, or any other AI risk.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are not mentioned.
just.regulation: He says "we should not stand in the way" of AI's efficiencies, which suggests a hands-off, light-touch stance. He names no specific policy, so this is a tentative read.

members.summary: Adrian Smith speaks about AI in strongly positive terms, focusing on the economic efficiencies it already delivers. He argues that policymakers should not obstruct it and should celebrate its benefits. The single statement gives no view on AGI, catastrophic risk, China, or specific regulations.

members.name: Christopher H. Smith

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as a tool of authoritarian surveillance and propaganda, and as a source of burdens on communities through data centers. He notes AI-related investment will create jobs (s5), but harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or AI reshaping society at a transformative scale. His remarks cover surveillance, propaganda, and data centers only.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday and geopolitical harms: surveillance, deepfake propaganda, and the burdens of data centers. None are catastrophic or loss-of-control framings.
just.china_race: China recurs in his AI statements, mainly as a surveillance and propaganda threat, and once explicitly as a 'tight race for technological dominance'. The race is not the dominant lens, and it is balanced against other concerns such as local data center impacts.
just.regulation: He backs specific measures, such as the Ratepayer Protection Act, which requires data centers to pay for their energy use, and he supports community voice in data center siting. There is no sign of a broad AI regulatory framework.

members.summary: Smith mostly discusses AI as a tool the Chinese Communist Party uses for surveillance, repression, and propaganda, including against Uyghurs and Taiwan. More recently he has focused on AI data centers, criticizing their strain on local resources and ratepayers and backing a targeted bill to make large energy users pay. He also describes a tight technology race with China, but he does not talk about AGI or catastrophic AI risk.

members.name: Linda T. Sánchez

just.ai_overall: She praises a student AI app and attends an industry dialogue, but these are brief and don't state an overall view of AI. The disinformation remark is about new technologies in general, not AI specifically.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements mention AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformative impact.
just.x_risk: She raises only disinformation from new technologies, and doesn't discuss catastrophic or existential AI risk. The statement is also not explicitly about AI, so it is too thin to score a 1.
just.china_race: China and AI competition are not mentioned in any statement.
just.regulation: She mentions working on digital policy, including trade, and offering an amendment on disinformation, but takes no clear position on AI regulation.

members.summary: Sánchez speaks about AI rarely and in general terms. She highlights a constituent student's AI public-speaking app and mentions a dialogue with tech leaders on AI and digital policy. She also warns that new technologies are used to spread disinformation, without tying this clearly to AI.

members.name: Bennie G. Thompson

just.ai_overall: He pairs real opportunity (using AI for security, education exposure, harnessing its potential) with real risks (adversary use, election manipulation, discrimination). The balance is roughly even, with an emphasis on responsible development.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is advancing rapidly and mentions a 'new AI era', but never discusses AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation in a way that fits the rubric. The statements mostly treat AI as a security and policy issue.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security risks such as adversaries using AI against critical infrastructure, cyberattacks, and election integrity. He never raises loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: He worries about 'adversaries' using AI and foreign influence operations, but never frames AI as a race with China. China is not named, and the concern is defensive security.
just.regulation: He backs standards-based, evidence-driven AI rules and criticizes the ad hoc approach of the current administration. He also supports specific measures such as a CISA AI task force, civil rights and privacy protections, and tools to detect manipulated content, rather than a broad framework.

members.summary: Thompson mostly discusses AI through homeland security, cybersecurity, and election integrity, stressing both its defensive potential and its use by adversaries. He supports responsible, standards-based oversight and protections for civil rights and privacy, and criticizes the Trump administration's ad hoc approach. He also welcomes AI education exposure for students, but does not discuss AGI, existential risk, or an AI race with China.

members.name: Mike Thompson

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges some benefits, such as AI tools improving health diagnoses, but nearly all his statements stress harms: job displacement, privacy, fraud, weaponization, and chatbot risks. He calls AI 'advancing at an uncontrolled pace'.
just.agi_pilled: He refers to 'advanced artificial intelligence' and a 'rapidly evolving technology' but never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation.
just.x_risk: He flags large-scale risks including mass cybersecurity breaches, biological or chemical weapons, weaponization, and 'catastrophic risk' from advanced AI. He does not explicitly discuss loss of control, though 'uncontrolled pace' and 'threaten us all' point toward it.
just.china_race: He says the U.S. can still lead the world in AI while setting guardrails, and wants the U.S. to lead on a global framework. China is never named and the race is not a major theme.
just.regulation: He pushes hard for Congress to pass bipartisan AI safety guardrails and calls for the House to be reconvened for urgent action. He also supports a global safety framework and conditions on data centers. His proposals are not yet specific licensing or agency-level measures.

members.summary: Thompson speaks about AI mostly in terms of risk. He cites job losses, privacy, fraud, chatbot harms to kids, cyberattacks, and bioweapons, and he calls for urgent congressional safeguards and an international safety framework. He credits AI with some health benefits and says the U.S. can stay a leader, and he is skeptical of rapid data center buildout and wants local control.

members.name: Glenn Thompson

just.ai_overall: He calls AI an incredible opportunity and says it is here to stay, but he also stresses risks, guardrails, and the burdens data centers place on communities. The balance is roughly even.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements mention AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation. They cover AI in schools, consumer protection, and data center siting.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises are everyday ones: AI-generated images, bullying, effects on special needs students, and consumer harm. None are catastrophic or involve loss of control.
just.china_race: China and international competition never come up in the statements.
just.regulation: He supports guardrails, guidelines, and oversight, with safeguards in place before major data center projects go forward. His proposals are general or targeted, such as consumer protection and siting, and do not amount to a broad framework such as licensing or liability.

members.summary: Glenn Thompson describes AI as an incredible opportunity and an evolving technology that is here to stay, especially for education, where he says it should help teachers rather than replace them. He keeps returning to risk management, consumer protection, and 'do no harm.' He is particularly wary of data centers, citing farmland, the grid, and rural communities. His concerns are practical rather than catastrophic.

members.name: John Thune

just.ai_overall: He calls AI revolutionary, with large benefits for health care, agriculture and logistics, and he stresses innovation and leadership. He also acknowledges real threats and risks that guardrails should manage, so he reads as mostly optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a "revolutionary technology" with broad impact across industries, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence. That fits transformative without AGI.
just.x_risk: His concerns are transparency, accountability, deceptive AI content, Russian bot-farm disinformation, and unspecified "more advanced threats". He gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: He says "we are in a race with China" and that staying ahead in the AI race is important. This is a recurring theme but balanced with guardrails, not used to oppose all rules.
just.regulation: He backs a bipartisan, risk-based framework with transparency and guardrails for high-impact AI, while insisting on a light touch with no burdensome audits or licensing. He is wary of FTC or agency regulation. That is targeted rules, not broad ones.

members.summary: Thune presents AI as a revolutionary technology with large economic and social benefits, and he says the U.S. must stay ahead of China. He consistently favors a light-touch approach modeled on internet policy. He also champions a bipartisan bill with transparency and risk-based guardrails for the highest-impact AI systems, without audits or licensing. He does not discuss AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Paul Tonko

just.ai_overall: He praises AI's potential for health care, research, and the economy, and also warns about jobs, security, inequity, data center costs, and AI use in insurance. The two sides are roughly balanced, with the concerns growing more prominent in 2026.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will 'revolutionize' health care, manufacturing, and the economy, and that we have 'only begun to scratch the surface.' That is transformative language, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: jobs, inequity, data collection by sportsbooks, insurance denials, and electricity costs. He says Congress shouldn't wait for an 'AI disaster,' but he does not describe a catastrophic or loss-of-control scenario.
just.china_race: China appears only indirectly, through export controls and a general call for American leadership and competitiveness. Race framing is not a main theme of his AI statements.
just.regulation: He demands that Congress 'rein in AI' now. He also supports guardrails and safety nets, minimum standards for AI use by sportsbooks, and a data center surcharge and cost protections. This goes beyond narrow fixes, though he has not proposed licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Paul Tonko describes AI as a source of economic and research opportunity, especially in health care, semiconductors, and education and workforce training. Since 2025 his tone has become more urgent. He now calls for guardrails and for Congress to 'rein in AI,' and he focuses on data center costs for consumers, AI in Medicare decisions, and AI-driven data use by gambling companies. He does not discuss AGI or existential risk, and China appears mainly through export controls and competitiveness.

members.name: Michael R. Turner

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as one of the most important developments and wants the U.S. to harness its full potential for growth, security and daily life. He also names risks, such as authoritarian use and military decision-making, but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI and quantum are reshaping the world and calls AI one of the most important developments, which implies large-scale transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He wants humans, not AI, to make any decision about nuclear weapons and to stay in charge in conflicts, which is a national-security catastrophe concern. He does not discuss loss of control of advanced AI. He also calls authoritarian use of AI a huge threat to freedom.
just.china_race: He calls adversaries getting to AI first the biggest threat and cites China and Russia investing in AI as a reason for the U.S. to harness it. Competition with adversaries is a primary lens, though he does not use it to argue against all constraints.
just.regulation: None of the statements address regulating AI companies or AI rules. The only related remark is a norm that humans keep control of nuclear and military decisions, which is not a regulatory proposal.

members.summary: Turner talks about AI mainly in national-security and geopolitical terms. He calls it an important analytical tool and stresses that the U.S. must stay ahead of adversaries such as China and Russia. He also says humans should keep decision-making authority over nuclear weapons and warfare. He says little about domestic AI regulation or advanced-AI scenarios.

members.name: Chris Van Hollen

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mostly as a threat, citing frontier risks, job losses, higher electricity costs, and military misuse. His only pro-innovation remark is a brief 2022 line, so harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He says frontier AI poses risks to all of humanity and that AI is a looming threat to the workforce. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI, so the evidence supports only a sense of a significant, high-stakes technology.
just.x_risk: He says frontier AI poses 'risks for all of humanity' and 'catastrophic harm,' cites models that 'broke containment,' and wants to protect humanity from unregulated development. This is a real loss-of-control concern, though he does not use explicit extinction language or compare it to nuclear war.
just.china_race: He rejects the race framing, saying the administration uses China to scare people out of limiting AI. He calls for urgent dialogue and mutual safeguards with China, though he also worries about chip transfers reaching China.
just.regulation: He calls for mandatory safeguards, a comprehensive testing regime, and liability for AI companies. He wants to pump the brakes on frontier development, says GPT-6 Astra should be pulled from public use, and opposes state preemption.

members.summary: Van Hollen talks about AI mainly as a danger that is unregulated and tied to Trump-administration corruption. He cites frontier-model safety incidents and risks to humanity, and he calls for mandatory testing, liability, and a slowdown of frontier development. He rejects the China-race argument against regulation, favoring negotiated safeguards with Beijing. He also raises data-center electricity costs, job losses, and military uses of AI.

members.name: Nydia M. Velázquez

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's potential (productivity, efficiency, revolutionizing government) with real risks (bias, security, threats to creators), in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: She calls AI 'the technological revolution of our lifetimes' and says its trajectory is unpredictable, which signals transformative change, but she never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday and sectoral: bias, misinformation, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, chatbot accuracy, and harm to small creators. She mentions unpredictable future risks but gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an international AI race.
just.regulation: She supports targeted measures: safeguards for federal agency AI tools, SBA reporting on AI use and risks, and help for small businesses to evaluate AI. She does not call for broad frameworks or licensing.

members.summary: Velázquez talks about AI mainly through a small-business lens. She sees it as a major technological shift with real efficiency gains, and she stresses risks such as bias, security gaps, inaccurate outputs, and harm to small creators. Her policy approach is practical and incremental: safeguards for federal AI use, SBA reporting requirements, and education for small businesses.

members.name: Tim Walberg

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as an opportunity that will create more opportunity for Americans and that should be allowed to develop. He also names manageable concerns: kids' safety, academic integrity, entry-level jobs, and fraud.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is rapidly transforming and reshaping the workforce, education, and the economy, and that it is scaling quickly. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday ones: fraud, criminal use, kids, academic integrity, job changes, and privacy. He raises no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: China appears repeatedly as a competitor and threat, with calls for U.S. leadership in AI and for America to set the standard. This sits alongside other concerns such as workforce, safety, and privacy, so it is not the dominant lens.
just.regulation: He favors a light touch, warns that government standards will restrict AI, and says not to rush into sweeping rules. He accepts some guardrails against fraud and harms to kids, and backs a data-gathering bill.

members.summary: Walberg talks about AI mainly through workforce, education, and economic competitiveness, and he is generally optimistic that it will create opportunity. He accepts limited guardrails on fraud and child safety but prefers a light-touch approach over sweeping rules. He frames China as a strategic competitor and says U.S. leadership matters. He does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Debbie Wasserman Schultz

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's potential with concrete harms: AI can counter hatred but also spreads animus, and offers great potential but needs guardrails to protect creativity. She says AI is 'not inherently good or evil.'
just.agi_pilled: She compares the AI revolution to automobiles replacing horse-drawn wagons and says AI is still in its 'Model-T era.' That implies large transformation but no mention of AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: online antisemitism, threats to creative work, and AI-driven heartlessness. She mentions 'unforeseen harm' only generically, with no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an international AI race.
just.regulation: She supports 'responsible regulations' and 'guardrails,' especially for creative work and online hate. She does not call for broad frameworks, licensing, or frontier-model rules.

members.summary: Wasserman Schultz describes AI as a tool whose effects depend on who builds and uses it. She focuses on its role in spreading online antisemitism and on guardrails for the arts, while also saying it can counter hate. She calls AI early-stage but potentially as transformative as the automobile, and she backs responsible regulation without detailing broad proposals.

members.name: Maxine Waters

just.ai_overall: Her statements frame AI almost entirely as a threat: harm to children, discrimination, job loss, and systemic financial risk. She names no benefits and calls the threat 'already here'.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is growing more powerful and could disrupt major systems. She never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or transformation on the scale of the internet or the industrial revolution.
just.x_risk: She refers to 'novel and existential AI risks' to the financial system and warns AI could disrupt government and markets. The framing centers on systemic and national-security risk, not loss of control over advanced AI.
just.china_race: China appears only in the context of outbound investment screening and keeping U.S. money from helping Chinese military or AI development. She does not frame AI policy as a race, and it is a minor theme.
just.regulation: She calls for regulation right away. She opposes preemption of state laws and regulatory sandboxes, and backs transparency and disclosure requirements and oversight of Big Tech. This goes beyond narrow targeted fixes, though she does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Maxine Waters talks about AI mainly as a source of risk. She points to discriminatory algorithms, harm to children, job displacement, and threats to the financial system. She pushes for stronger oversight and transparency, opposes Republican deregulation efforts such as regulatory sandboxes and federal preemption of state laws, and criticizes Big Tech. China comes up only in narrow national-security and investment contexts.

members.name: Daniel Webster

just.ai_overall: He sees AI and automation as something to explore, for example when labor is short, while also noting the risks and system failures that come with it. The statements are brief and lean neither clearly optimistic nor clearly concerned.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation from AI. The statements only discuss specific applications such as automation and autonomous vessels.
just.x_risk: He raises operational risks such as cybersecurity problems, collision avoidance, and unpredictable system failures. None of these is framed as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: He repeatedly asks about China's influence on AI standards and about protecting American critical-technology research. China is a recurring theme in his questions, though he does not use explicit race language or argue against constraints.
just.regulation: He asks about international technical standards and about evaluating risks. He takes no clear position on whether to regulate AI domestically.

members.summary: Webster talks about AI mostly in hearing questions about specific uses, including automation in industry and autonomous vessels. He notes that new technology brings risks that must be evaluated. He also repeatedly asks about China's role in AI standards and protecting American technology research. He does not state broad positions on AGI or regulation.

members.name: Peter Welch

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly calls AI's potential enormous and transformative, and backs beneficial uses like weather forecasting and help for farmers. He pairs this with concerns about deception, copyright, privacy and warfare, and says AI needs guardrails, so the balance is mixed.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will vastly transform the economy, comparing it to the telegraph and the internet. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He warns that AI in warfare will soon drive global instability, which is a large-scale security risk. He also says he is 'freaked out' by AI researchers' warnings, but he never describes loss of control or extinction.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race with China. The only 'arms race' reference is about data.
just.regulation: He supports an independent expert agency for AI and digital platforms, licensing with independent testing before AI systems are built, and opposes federal preemption and moratoria on state laws. He also backs consent, transparency and copyright measures.

members.summary: Welch describes AI as a transformative technology on the scale of the internet. He sees real benefits, such as better weather forecasting and help for farmers, and he stresses risks including deepfakes in elections, data scraping, artists' rights and military instability. He is a consistent advocate of strong oversight: an independent AI agency, licensing and testing, and opposition to preempting state laws.

members.name: Joe Wilson

just.ai_overall: He says AI so far has been 'substantially very good,' producing efficiency and jobs, and he stresses its economic benefits. He also supports limiting bad actors' misuse, so he sees risks as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI. He talks about a 'large boost to economic productivity,' which does not clearly signal expectations of radical transformation.
just.x_risk: He cosponsored a bill meant to 'eliminate catastrophic risk' and talks about stopping bad actors from using AI to do harm. This points to concern about serious misuse, but he never mentions loss of control.
just.china_race: He says 'we cannot allow China to win the global AI race' and ties US AI leadership to national security. He also describes China's military-civilian fusion as the adversary. The race is a primary lens, though he does not use it to argue against all regulation.
just.regulation: He backs a bipartisan framework with 'sensible regulation' to spur innovation and prevent catastrophic risk. He also supports targeted legislation against bad actors and a ratepayer protection bill. This amounts to targeted, light-to-moderate rules rather than broad frameworks.

members.summary: Joe Wilson speaks about AI mostly in positive terms, as a source of efficiency, jobs and economic productivity. He frames it largely through national security and competition with China, including defense cooperation with Israel. He supports bipartisan bills with 'sensible regulation' against catastrophic risk and bad actors, while admitting he is not an expert on the issue.

members.name: Frederica S. Wilson

just.ai_overall: The single statement says no one has a handle on AI but does not say whether she sees it as mainly promising or harmful.
just.agi_pilled: She says nothing about AGI, superintelligence, or how transformative AI will be.
just.x_risk: She does not mention catastrophic, existential, or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: China and any AI race are not mentioned.
just.regulation: She suggests that more than one party needs to be involved, but it is unclear whether she means both parties or government and industry. She states no position on regulation.

members.summary: The only available statement is a brief 2023 remark that no one has a real handle on AI or the right prescription, so multiple groups need to be involved. It shows humility about the uncertainty but gives no view on benefits, risks, China, or specific rules.

members.name: Robert J. Wittman

just.ai_overall: He pairs 'immense potential' and 'impressive advancements' with 'serious harm' without proper regulation, plus concerns about deepfakes and data-center costs. Promise and risk appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'powerful new force' and part of a 'monumental change' in how the nation defends itself, which suggests large-scale transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His stated concerns are everyday harms: deepfake exploitation of children, serious harm without regulation, and energy costs. None are framed as catastrophic or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: He refers to 'adversaries' and military advantage in a defense context but never names China or frames AI as a race. That is too thin to score.
just.regulation: He backs thoughtful, responsible regulation and guardrails, and supports a specific bill. His concrete concerns are targeted: deepfake exploitation of children and data-center ratepayer costs.

members.summary: Wittman describes AI as a powerful force with real promise, especially for national security and the economy, and he stresses the need for thoughtful guardrails. His concerns are concrete: deepfake harms to children and data-center energy costs falling on ratepayers. He frames AI in defense as a major shift, and he does not discuss AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Steve Womack

just.ai_overall: He calls AI a critical technology that will benefit Americans and drive the economy, and he promotes its practical uses. He acknowledges job changes and the need for guardrails, but treats risks as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will touch nearly every sector of the economy and change how many jobs are performed, which suggests broad transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence, and he likens the change to earlier technological advances.
just.x_risk: He mentions guardrails and adversaries with nefarious intentions, but never describes catastrophic, existential, or loss-of-control risks, and he doesn't discuss specific everyday harms either.
just.china_race: He worries that over-regulating would cede technology to adversaries, and he links AI to defense. China is never named and the race framing is not a recurring or dominant theme, so this is a modest presence balanced with support for guardrails.
just.regulation: He wants regulation that does not stifle innovation and prefers partnership with industry. He accepts some guardrails and a role for Congress but warns against going too far.

members.summary: Steve Womack talks about AI as a beneficial, economy-boosting technology and often points to local uses in logistics, agriculture, and defense in Arkansas. He supports some congressional guardrails but repeatedly cautions against rules that would stifle innovation or let adversaries gain an edge. His statements do not address AGI, catastrophic risk, or specific harms.

members.name: Ron Wyden

just.ai_overall: Wyden mostly frames AI through harms: bias, surveillance, automated care denials, and market consolidation. He briefly acknowledges 'exciting opportunities' (s11) and wants agencies to use new tech, but the harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is growing rapidly across every industry and that tech is advancing fast, but he never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or civilizational-scale change. His statements are about specific current uses, so the evidence is too thin to place him on this scale.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: bias, surveillance, privacy, health-care denials, and concentration of market power. None involve catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race. He discusses AI substantively, but the framing never comes up.
just.regulation: He sponsors the Algorithmic Accountability Act requiring bias testing and transparency, says AI chatbots lack Section 230 protection and companies should be liable, opposes the state-law moratorium, and calls for new rules on AI surveillance. This is substantial, though not licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Wyden talks about AI mainly as a civil-liberties, consumer-protection, and fairness issue. He focuses on algorithmic bias, AI-driven surveillance using commercially purchased data, automated insurance and Medicare denials, and Big Tech concentration. He has backed bills for algorithm audits and transparency, opposed a federal preemption of state AI laws, and says 'new tools require new rules'. He acknowledges AI's opportunities only briefly and does not discuss AGI, existential risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Todd Young

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as an economic, scientific and security opportunity, and says Congress should harness benefits while mitigating risks. He warns against over-regulating and mentions risks only briefly.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as fundamentally transforming the economy, security and global power, and as a 'revolution' and 'foundational technology'. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: He raises national-security threats from advanced AI, AI-biosecurity links and 'dystopian' constituent concerns. He does not discuss loss of control or extinction risk, and his risk language is general.
just.china_race: Beating China in AI is a recurring, primary lens, from 'must prevail in the AI race against China' to standards-setting and limiting Chinese access to labs. He also cites other concerns such as American values, so it does not fully override everything else.
just.regulation: He favors voluntary standards, a single federal standard with narrow state exceptions, and removing regulatory barriers, and he warns about the opportunity cost of over-regulating. He backs a narrow deepfake-related bill and some guardrails.

members.summary: Todd Young talks about AI mainly as an engine of innovation, economic growth and national security. He often says the U.S. must lead and out-compete China, and he stresses American-values standards, research investment (CREATE AI Act), workforce education and the Future of AI Innovation Act. He acknowledges risks and supports voluntary standards, a federal framework and a few targeted guardrails, but he warns against over-regulation and does not discuss AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Mark E. Amodei

just.ai_overall: Both statements describe AI applications in positive terms (access to legal help, support for armed forces and disaster relief) and mention no harms. The evidence is thin and promotional, so the score is mostly optimistic and stops short of very optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: The statements discuss specific AI tools and say nothing about AGI or economy-wide transformation. Two brief statements are too few to conclude he sees AI as ordinary technology.
just.x_risk: Neither statement discusses AI risks of any kind, catastrophic or everyday.
just.china_race: China and any AI race are never mentioned. The national security reference is only about supporting the armed forces with a specific product.
just.regulation: Neither statement takes a position on AI rules or oversight.

members.summary: Amodei's two statements present AI favorably and in practical terms: AI-powered drones for national security and disaster relief, and AI tools in libraries that help low-income Nevadans with legal information. He does not discuss risks, regulation, AGI, or competition with China in these statements.

members.name: Suzanne Bonamici

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's 'tremendous potential' with 'significant risks' and treats the two in roughly equal measure. Her recent statements lean toward risk and safeguards, but she still names benefits such as disaster preparedness.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is 'reshaping the workforce faster than we can respond' and is reshaping learning and work. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence, so this reads as very transformative but not AGI-focused.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: bias, privacy, job displacement, deepfakes, critical thinking and security breaches. One remark that 'powerful models don't cause the next disaster' is vague and does not describe catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. She only criticizes the administration's framing of AI leadership as a race focused on speed and deployment, and argues it needs trust and preparation.
just.regulation: She says companies 'don't get to regulate themselves' and calls for clear rules and accountability. She opposes the state-law moratorium, backs hiring-discrimination legislation and the No Robot Bosses Act, and is developing a comprehensive framework. This goes beyond narrow fixes but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Bonamici describes AI as holding great potential and significant risks, and she stresses 'human-centered' safeguards, especially in education, hiring and the workforce. She opposes the federal moratorium on state AI laws, supports accountability and transparency rules, and is developing a comprehensive framework. She does not discuss AGI, existential risk or competition with China, apart from criticizing the administration's race framing.

members.name: Suzan K. DelBene

just.ai_overall: Most of her recent AI statements frame AI as a harm, specifically its use to delay and deny Medicare care. She does acknowledge some benefits, such as small businesses using AI to grow, a student's AI project, and AI that can 'advance care'. Harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or AI reshaping society on a historic scale. Her comments cover specific uses and privacy.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: privacy, deepfakes, and denial of health care. One mention of 'the threat AI poses, according to the very people building these programs' and national security is vague and not framed as catastrophic or loss of control.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned. The closest is a general wish for the U.S. to lead and have a seat at the international table.
just.regulation: She backs substantial rules: a national privacy law as the foundation for AI guardrails, national AI safeguards, and legislation to cancel the AI Medicare prior-authorization program. She also pushes for transparency and accountability. This goes beyond narrow fixes but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: DelBene's early AI comments (2023–24) focus on passing a national data privacy law as the first step toward AI guardrails, with some attention to deepfakes. From late 2025 on, nearly all her AI statements attack the Trump administration's WISeR program, which pays private companies to use AI to review Medicare claims, and which she says delays and denies seniors' care. She calls for national AI safeguards, transparency, and repeal of that program, and she says she wants AI used responsibly. She says nothing about AGI, catastrophic risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Thomas Massie

just.ai_overall: He says he loves AI and is not anti-AI, and he champions open, user-owned AI as a tool for liberty. He also worries about government censorship AI, corporate favoritism, AI-driven bots, and deceptive AI political ads, but he treats these as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He talks about AI as a tool, as bots, and as a policy fight over data centers. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence, and he never says AI will transform society on a massive scale. He mocks claims that AI will kill us, but he does not address AGI directly.
just.x_risk: He mocks 'AI is going to kill us' claims as coming from the people making AI, and he says AI should not be treated like nuclear weapons. He accepts only ordinary dangers, comparing them to fire.
just.china_race: No statement frames AI as a race or competition with China.
just.regulation: He opposes broad AI regulation, a new AI agency, and outlawing AI, and he voted against the TAKE IT DOWN Act. He calls regulation of 'math' futile and sees calls for it as a way to build barriers to entry. He also opposes the federal moratorium on state AI laws and the data-center exemptions, which keeps him from the strongest anti-regulation score.

members.summary: Massie describes himself as pro-AI ('I love AI'). He favors open, user-owned AI and warns that government and Big Tech will use AI for censorship and control. He is skeptical of AI regulation and dismisses AI doom talk. He opposed the federal ban on state AI laws and the data-center exemptions, mainly on grounds of local control and corporate favoritism. He often calls out suspected AI bots and AI-generated political ads.

members.name: Brian Schatz

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges AI's promise (weather prediction, government services, 'amazing possibilities'), but most of his statements stress harms: scams, misinformation, risks to kids, and rogue models. By 2026 he describes the risk as 'acute' and calls for emergency action, so harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI grows more advanced daily and that it could become too powerful for any one actor to manage. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation, so there is not enough to place him.
just.x_risk: He says models are 'escaping human control' and backs a bill to keep humans in control. He says he won't tolerate a 2–10% chance of catastrophic risk, which makes loss of control a real concern. He does not explicitly compare it to nuclear war or pandemics.
just.china_race: China appears only once, in a remark about the PRC exporting facial-recognition AI for repression. Race framing does not feature in his AI statements.
just.regulation: He backs mandatory labeling and says Big Tech can't self-police. He also calls for pre-deployment and third-party testing, supports the AI Safety Institute, and wants to hold AI companies accountable. He opposes preempting state laws without a federal standard. He goes beyond targeted rules but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Schatz talks about AI mostly as a consumer-protection and safety problem. For years his signature issue was the bipartisan AI Labeling Act to counter scams, deepfakes and misinformation, along with kids' safety and worker protections. By late 2026 he frames AI risk as acute and catastrophic, citing models escaping human control, and pushes for mandatory testing and urgent bipartisan action. He opposes federal preemption of state AI laws and criticizes Congress for inaction.

members.name: Bill Foster

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly says the goal is to both harness AI's potential and protect against its dangers, and he celebrates AI supercomputers and research. Since 2025 his statements are dominated by risk and calls for urgency, so the balance is mixed, tilting toward concern.
just.agi_pilled: He talks about AGI that can outperform humans at most tasks, about superhuman AI, and about recursive self-improvement. He calls AI a coming 'freight train' and says agentic AI will 'change everything'. He gives no explicit timeline, so this stops short of the top score.
just.x_risk: He warns that AI agents that rewrite themselves could evade human oversight, and says superhuman AI needs nuclear-style physical containment. He also flags AI-enabled bioweapons. He does not frame extinction as the top priority, but loss of control is clearly a real concern for him.
just.china_race: He cares about staying ahead of China ('we cannot be in second place') and about keeping advanced chips out of Chinese hands through his Chip Security Act. He also calls for talks with China on AI safeguards and international coordination, so race framing is present but balanced.
just.regulation: He strongly and repeatedly urges Congress to pass 'comprehensive' and 'technically feasible' AI legislation. He backs chip-tracking requirements and says companies' calls to 'deliberately pace' AI deserve attention. His concrete bills are fairly targeted (labeling, chips, financial oversight), so this stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Bill Foster, a physicist and chip designer on the House AI Task Force, talks about AI as a technology with real promise whose risks Congress is neglecting. His early focus was deepfakes, digital identity, and financial-sector risks. By 2025–26 he stresses agentic AI destabilizing banks, recursive self-improvement, rogue AI agents, and containing superhuman AI. He pushes for technically grounded legislation, chip export security, and some international coordination, including with China.

members.name: Dina Titus

just.ai_overall: She promotes beneficial AI uses (emergency vehicles, wildfire tracking, scam protection for seniors) while voicing worries about AI replacing workers and making safety-critical decisions. Benefits and risks look roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: Her statements treat AI as a practical tool and a labor or safety issue. None mention AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday ones: job displacement, safety in air traffic control and rail, and environmental effects of data centers. None are framed as catastrophic or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: She introduced the RESTRICT Act to protect U.S. 'dominance in the AI race' by blocking advanced chip sales to China. The theme appears only once among other concerns such as labor, safety, and the environment, so it is present but not dominant.
just.regulation: She supports specific oversight and rules: congressional oversight of AI in air traffic control, environmental assessment and transparency for data centers, and chip export controls. She does not describe a broad framework or licensing regime.

members.summary: Titus discusses AI mostly in practical, district-focused terms. She celebrates federal grants and local projects that use AI for road safety, wildfire tracking, cybersecurity training, and helping seniors. She also stresses oversight and worker protection, opposing AI replacing rail workers or controlling air traffic, and calls for public review of data center impacts. She backs export controls on AI chips to China to keep U.S. dominance in the AI race.

members.name: Tom Cotton

just.ai_overall: He mostly describes AI as a strategic and economic opportunity, citing cures for cancer, law-enforcement benefits and national prosperity. His concerns are narrower: chips going to China, data-center energy costs, harms to children, and perceived political bias in AI systems.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI dominance critical and talks about the AI race, but he never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation. His statements treat AI mainly as a strategic technology and economic asset.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns are about adversaries obtaining advanced chips and technology, child safety, fraud, and bias. None of his statements address loss of control or existential risk. The national-security framing concerns geopolitical competition, not a catastrophic misuse scenario like bioweapons.
just.china_race: Beating China is his dominant lens and recurs in most of his statements, including chip export controls, bans on Chinese models, and data-center policy. He also argues that federal control of AI would be a disaster, though he does support targeted security-related restrictions.
just.regulation: He opposes broad federal control of AI and says legislation should be targeted and straightforward, with narrow guardrails on child safety, fraud and vulnerable people. He supports export controls, chip security, and accountability for AI that preys on children, but is wary of broader regulation and favors deregulating power for data centers.

members.summary: Tom Cotton talks about AI mostly as a contest with China, and he calls American AI dominance vital to national security and prosperity. He backs export controls, chip-security legislation, and bans on Chinese AI tools, and he wants data-center growth without higher electricity prices. He favors only narrow, targeted guardrails such as protecting children, opposes broad federal control of AI, and accuses AI systems and the Biden administration of anti-conservative bias.

members.name: Jared Huffman

just.ai_overall: He is mostly critical of AI's buildout, citing higher electric bills, water use, fossil fuel reliance, and DOGE's use of AI. He acknowledges limited benefits (an AI math app, and 'we do need that' for grid improvements).
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformative potential. The statements are about data centers, energy, and government use of AI.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday and infrastructure harms: electricity costs, water, climate, and AI-driven layoffs. None involve catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned in the statements.
just.regulation: He backs 'common-sense guardrails' on AI data centers and wants to 'pump the brakes' on the buildout. These are targeted measures on data centers and energy, not a broad framework for AI companies.

members.summary: Huffman talks about AI mainly through data centers: their energy demand, electricity bills, water use, fossil fuel reliance, and climate effects. He is critical of the Trump administration's AI buildout and of DOGE's use of AI, though he says grid improvements are needed and has praised an AI learning app. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: Ami Bera

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly praises AI's promise, especially in health care, and pairs it with worries about workforce displacement, AI threats, and the need for guardrails. Promise and risk get roughly equal weight.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will 'rapidly transform' health care and that it is moving fast. He does not mention AGI or superintelligence. The passing remark about 'AI thinking on its own' is too thin to show AGI expectations.
just.x_risk: He flags AI-related national security risks, such as military and intelligence misuse and crisis escalation with China, and wants guardrails and crisis channels. He also says he worries about 'AI thinking on its own,' but only briefly, so loss of control is not clearly a major concern.
just.china_race: Protecting America's technological edge over China is a recurring theme, shown in his chip-export bills. He balances it with calls for dialogue and crisis communication with China on AI safety, so he does not treat the race as dominant.
just.regulation: He consistently calls for guardrails and safeguards, urgent congressional action, and a federal framework built on state efforts such as California's. He backs congressional approval for chip sales and guardrails on military AI. These are substantive measures, though he does not propose licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Ami Bera, a physician, describes AI as promising, particularly for health care, and argues that Congress must add guardrails. He urges bipartisan action and a federal framework informed by state laws. On China, he wants to protect the U.S. technological edge through chip-export oversight while also pressing for dialogue and crisis communication on AI safety.

members.name: Julia Brownley

just.ai_overall: She is enthusiastic about AI's potential, especially for VA systems ('I believe this very, very strongly'), and says VA must not be left behind. She also acknowledges real risks, such as lost human touch in healthcare, and favors a balanced approach. Overall she leans optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI will be 'very, very important' and will change how we live, but she never mentions AGI or human-level AI. Nothing indicates whether she expects change on the scale of the internet or beyond.
just.x_risk: The risks she names are everyday ones, like reduced patient trust and outcomes when the human element is removed, plus general 'real risks.' She does bring up national security in connection with technology regulation, but she describes no catastrophic or loss-of-control scenario.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned in these statements.
just.regulation: She supports a new government technology agency to advise Congress, and she backs a measured, pilot-program approach to AI. Her comments are mostly about institutional capacity and specific applications, not a broad regulatory framework.

members.summary: Brownley talks about AI mostly in a Veterans Affairs and healthcare context. She is optimistic about its potential to modernize VA systems and wants veterans not to be left behind. She also warns about losing the human element in care and favors balanced, measured steps like pilot programs and a new tech advisory agency.

members.name: Raul Ruiz

just.ai_overall: He wants AI to be built responsibly and equitably and says the US can lead in AI. He also raises strong concerns about kids' safety, mental health harms, deepfakes, and data center impacts, so promise and risk look roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or AI on the scale of the industrial revolution. He treats AI as a set of specific products and infrastructure issues.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: kids' privacy, chatbot mental-health risks, deepfakes, and data center costs and health effects. None are framed as catastrophic or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: China appears once, in a criticism of Trump's stance on the CHIPS Act and US competitiveness in AI. It is not a recurring lens in his AI statements.
just.regulation: He backs enforceable rules in several areas: FEC-enforced deepfake bans, kids' privacy and AI rules for minors, guardrails for mental-health chatbots, and federal environmental review and efficiency standards for data centers. Together these go beyond a single narrow fix, though he doesn't call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Ruiz talks about AI mainly through concrete harms and community impacts: kids' safety and privacy, chatbot mental-health risks, election deepfakes, and the energy, water, and health costs of data centers. He supports enforceable rules and oversight in each area while also saying he wants AI built responsibly and equitably, and that the US can lead. He does not discuss AGI or existential risk, and he mentions China only in passing.

members.name: Mark Takano

just.ai_overall: He calls AI 'more of an opportunity than a threat' and sees promise in education, but he also stresses inequitable gains, worker displacement, and corporations profiting at workers' expense. The overall picture is balanced, leaning slightly positive.
