just.regulation: She favors unleashing energy, data centers, and investment, and criticizes a data center moratorium and regulatory barriers. Her only caution is about academic integrity, and she backs a study commission rather than rules.

members.summary: Stefanik talks about AI mainly as an engine of economic growth and a national-security priority, and she often casts it as a race with China that the US must win. She backs investment, data centers, and military AI adoption, and she criticizes New York's data center moratorium. She notes smaller concerns such as adversary use of AI and student cheating, and she also mentions AI in political attacks over an opponent's AI-generated ad.

members.name: Brendan F. Boyle

just.ai_overall: The statements are jokes or dismissive quips about AI-generated content, plus a 2020 remark on automation in tax policy. None gives a clear overall view of AI's promise versus its harms.
just.agi_pilled: The 'AI taking over' quip is sarcastic, not a real view on AGI or transformative AI. Nothing else addresses AGI.
just.x_risk: The 'less worried about AI taking over' line is a joke about a poor-quality AI product, so it does not show a considered position on catastrophic risk.
just.china_race: No statement mentions China or an AI race.
just.regulation: No statement addresses AI regulation. The tax comment concerns the treatment of capital versus labor, not AI rules.

members.summary: Boyle's few statements touch on AI only in passing. He mocks low-quality AI-generated content on X and, in a 2020 hearing, raised how the tax code favors capital over labor and so encourages automation of jobs such as fast-food work. The record contains no substantive views on AI policy, AGI, catastrophic risk, China, or regulation.

members.name: Brian Babin

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as an economic and strategic opportunity, comparing it to electricity, and urges adoption and leadership. He acknowledges that AI brings risks and opportunities, but the risks are treated as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a general-purpose technology like electricity that will reshape every sector of the economy and national power, which is a very transformative framing. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns include AI-enabled cyberattacks, national security risks from the CCP, and critical infrastructure threats, plus support for nucleic acid screening legislation. He never discusses loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: Beating China is a dominant, recurring lens in his AI statements, and he often pairs it with arguments against heavy regulation and for removing barriers. He does not go as far as saying every constraint is a gift to Beijing, and he also says he wants to balance competitiveness with trustworthy systems.
just.regulation: He prefers voluntary standards, bottom-up consensus, and partnering with industry over aggressive regulation, and he warns against overregulation. He supports modest measures such as NIST resources and CAISI funding.

members.summary: Babin presents AI as a general-purpose technology on the scale of electricity and focuses on U.S. leadership, especially against the Chinese Communist Party. He stresses cutting barriers, building energy and data center capacity, and voluntary standards over aggressive regulation, while acknowledging cyber and national security risks. He does not discuss AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Donald S. Beyer, Jr.

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs AI's promise (health, science, productivity) with serious risks, for example 'AI has immense potential but we need to get this right.' His more recent statements stress risk and urgency, but he still describes benefits.
just.agi_pilled: He explicitly cites artificial superintelligence and AGI as things developers and policymakers must consider. He also refers to 'civilizational risks' and says AI is transformative. He gives no explicit timelines, so this stops short of a 4.
just.x_risk: He raises 'systemic and civilizational risks,' 'AI loss of control incidents,' and existential warnings from experts as real concerns requiring urgent action. Earlier (2024) he was unsure how real the existential risks were, but his recent statements treat them as serious.
just.china_race: China appears only occasionally, in criticism of Trump's chip-export decisions and a passing worry about 'ceding America's leadership.' Race framing is not a main lens for his AI policy.
just.regulation: He backs substantial federal rules: mandated testing and independent review, foundation-model transparency requirements, and a comprehensive federal framework. He rejects voluntary commitments and opposes preemption of state laws. He has not called for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Rep. Beyer presents himself as a legislator-student of AI who is pursuing a master's degree in machine learning. He consistently argues that AI offers real benefits but that Congress must set mandatory federal guardrails, because voluntary industry commitments fall short. His later statements stress urgency, citing AI-enabled cyberattacks, loss-of-control incidents, and superintelligence and civilizational risks. He also opposes federal preemption of state AI laws and attacks the Trump administration's approach as a 'Wild West.'

members.name: Stacey E. Plaskett

just.ai_overall: She describes AI's 'immense potential' and frames it as an opportunity for innovation and inclusion, while also flagging deepfake harms and calling for fairness and accountability. Her tone leans optimistic with manageable risks.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements discuss AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformation of society.
just.x_risk: Her only risk concerns are everyday harms: explicit deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, and fairness. None are catastrophic.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. The only competitive framing is a passing line about America leading in technology.
just.regulation: She backs targeted measures, namely a bipartisan deepfake/NCII bill that holds websites accountable, plus policies for transparency, accountability and fairness. She does not describe a broad regulatory framework.

members.summary: Plaskett talks about AI mostly in terms of equity, inclusion and opportunity, especially for Black and minority entrepreneurs and innovators. She co-leads bipartisan legislation against explicit deepfakes and non-consensual intimate imagery. Her statements do not address AGI, catastrophic risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Dan Newhouse

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as an engine of economic growth and a pillar of national security, and he is excited about agricultural applications. His only concern is about deepfakes in elections, so he comes across as mostly optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI an engine of economic growth with exponentially rising power demand and a cornerstone of national security, which suggests a large transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: The only risks he raises are election integrity and deepfakes, which are everyday harms. He gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: He talks about a 'race to lead the world in AI' and says electricity capacity will decide it. The race is a recurring frame but is tied to energy affordability and other concerns. China is not named, and he does not use the race to argue against all constraints.
just.regulation: He applauds a national AI framework and wants to codify it so that states cannot create a patchwork, which is a preemption stance. He also criticizes 'extreme' state legislatures. He does mention election integrity policy, so the stance is not fully anti-regulation.

members.summary: Newhouse speaks about AI mostly as an economic and national-security opportunity. He focuses on the electricity and data-center demand needed to win the AI race, and he highlights agricultural uses. He supports a federal framework that would override state AI rules and raises deepfakes and election integrity as his main concern.

members.name: Glenn Grothman

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs acknowledged benefits (productivity, efficiency, innovation) with worries about workers, students, privacy, and political bias. Neither side clearly dominates, so the view is balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He discusses AI many times, but only as a normal technology: workplace effects, privacy, education, data centers. Nothing suggests he expects AGI or radical transformation.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday ones: jobs, privacy, academic integrity, phony images, political bias, and surveillance-style control. He does not frame any risk as catastrophic or loss-of-control.
just.china_race: China appears only occasionally: once as an example of AI misuse for repression, and once in a passing reference to leading 'the AI race'. The race is not a main lens for his AI policy.
just.regulation: He supports targeted measures such as banning phony images, data-privacy and transparency rules, and the Ratepayer Protection Act for data centers. He is also wary of broad regulation, saying it benefits big companies and that less government is better.

members.summary: Grothman describes AI as a technology with real productivity benefits but with risks to workers, students, privacy, and fair political discourse. He favors careful, targeted action over broad regulation, backing rules on fake images, data oversight, and making data centers cover their own energy costs. He rarely frames AI in terms of AGI, catastrophic risk, or a race with China.

members.name: Dan Sullivan

just.ai_overall: Sullivan stresses AI's "enormous positive potential" and "immense" promise in health care and education, and he wants guardrails, especially for children. He treats risks as manageable through smart rules and by staying ahead of China.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI's promise "immense and transformative" and says it will transform health care and the economy. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: The risks he names are kids' safety, harms to communities, and Chinese military use of AI. None is framed as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: He repeatedly frames AI as a race with the Chinese Communist Party and presses witnesses on how to win it, including through energy production. He also pushes to restrict US investment in Chinese AI. He pairs this with some guardrails, so the race does not override everything else.
just.regulation: He backs targeted guardrails on kids' safety and wants AI companies to bear the costs of their data centers. He praises a framework with a uniform national policy that gives innovators certainty, which points toward light-touch rules rather than broad regulation.

members.summary: Sullivan talks about AI mainly as an economic, health-care, and military opportunity, and as a technology race with the Chinese Communist Party that the US must win. He supports guardrails, especially protecting children, and a uniform national policy, and he pushes for AI data centers and energy in Alaska. He does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk. Several statements attributed to him (the White House briefing, Biden–Xi and National Security Memorandum remarks) appear to come from a different Sullivan, and I did not rely on them.

members.name: Joni Ernst

just.ai_overall: She describes AI as helpful in medical research and defense and urges the country to embrace it. She also notes threats and wants guardrails, but she treats risks as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: She calls superintelligence a 'powerful tool' and speaks of systems that could 'go rogue.' She gives no timelines and does not describe AGI as imminent or central, so the evidence points to a moderate level of expectation for transformative AI.
just.x_risk: She says guardrails are needed so superintelligent systems 'cannot go rogue or be misused by our adversaries,' which acknowledges loss-of-control risk. She also flags AI-enabled cyberattacks as a national security threat. Her treatment of extinction-level risk is brief and not a top priority.
just.china_race: China competition is a recurring lens in her AI statements, and she uses it to argue against pausing or slowing AI. She still pairs it with some calls for guardrails, so it stops short of dominating everything else.
just.regulation: She rejects moratoria and wants guardrails that 'will not inhibit development and growth.' She favors light-touch, innovation-friendly rules, though she does back some targeted measures such as data center cost protections.

members.summary: Joni Ernst presents AI as a major opportunity for medicine, defense, and the economy, and she strongly opposes moratoria. Her framing is dominated by competition with China and by national security, including AI-enabled cyberattacks and the need to keep advanced systems from going rogue. She supports 'responsible guardrails' that don't stifle innovation, and she wants data centers built without raising costs for local ratepayers.

members.name: Thom Tillis

just.ai_overall: He says directly that "AI is good" and calls it a promising, positive disruptive technology. He also acknowledges real harms (likeness replication, threats to creators) and says guardrails are needed, but treats these as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He stresses the fast pace of change and the unpredictability of AI's future, and calls it a disruptive technology. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are mostly everyday harms such as IP, likeness, and cybersecurity. He treats the 'zombie apocalypse' fears lightly, and says guardrails matter and that AI isn't a 'hoax'. He never frames loss of control or extinction as a concern. His use of 'existential threat' refers only to creators.
just.china_race: He raises leadership in innovation and China's use of AI against cyber defenses. This is a recurring but modest theme, balanced against IP, safety, and other concerns.
just.regulation: He mostly backs targeted measures: NO FAKES, disclosure, AI security incident reporting, and federal procurement rules. He also supports industry self-regulation that could be codified, and says guardrails are needed, but he has not proposed broad frameworks or licensing.

members.summary: Tillis describes AI as a positive, disruptive technology and cites his own long background in it. He is mainly concerned with protecting creators' likeness and IP, with cybersecurity, and with keeping US leadership. He favors targeted legislation like NO FAKES and industry-led guardrails that Congress could codify, and he rejects the idea that AI risk is a hoax.

members.name: Mike Rounds

just.ai_overall: He mostly describes AI as a big opportunity, especially for curing diseases, the economy and defense, and says 'the sky is the limit.' He acknowledges dangers and the need for some guardrails, but treats the risks as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is changing the world 'as we know it,' will be 'the determining factor in all future great power competition,' and could cure major diseases within years. He introduced a bill for an Artificial General Intelligence Steering Committee, but only the bill title appears and he never discusses AGI or superintelligence in his own words.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns are national-security misuse: adversaries using AI to develop weapons such as biologics, and AI as a new cyber attack surface. He does not discuss loss of control or extinction risk, and he rejects a pause.
just.china_race: Beating China is a recurring and primary lens for him: 'We cannot lose this race,' and slowing down means China takes the lead. He uses the race to argue against pausing, though he also mentions kids' safety and oversight.
just.regulation: He favors a 'pro-innovative stance,' warns against overly broad rules, says existing laws and norms already apply to AI, and backs regulatory sandboxes. He accepts some targeted rules, such as kids' safety and oversight, and bipartisan roadmaps, but is wary of heavy regulation and opposes a pause.

members.summary: Rounds talks about AI as an unavoidable, largely beneficial technology that America must lead, especially for national defense, health care cures and economic growth. He frames AI heavily as a race with China and rejects slowing down. He supports bipartisan, innovation-friendly guardrails and mentions misuse risks such as bioweapons and cyberattacks, but he does not discuss existential risk or loss of control.

members.name: Trent Kelly

just.ai_overall: He supports funding AI for the military and defends data centers against what he calls a Chinese-driven negative narrative, which reads as an opportunity-focused view. He voices no concerns about AI itself, so the score stops short of 4 given how little evidence there is.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation. They cover only military funding and data centers.
just.x_risk: He discusses no AI risks, catastrophic or everyday. The only risk he raises is Chinese influence on public opinion.
just.china_race: He says China wants to lead in AI and data centers and is working to undermine U.S. data center buildout. This makes competition with China a primary lens for his view of data centers.
just.regulation: He does not discuss AI regulation. He mentions only NDAA funding and criticism of data center opposition.

members.summary: Kelly talks about AI mainly in terms of national security and competition with China. He backs AI funding for the military in the NDAA and says Chinese social media campaigns are driving opposition to U.S. data centers so that China can lead in AI. The statements say little about AI risks, AGI, or regulation.

members.name: Darin LaHood

just.ai_overall: He says AI has "so much promise" but also "peril" and stresses balance. He mostly frames it as a strategic opportunity to win and praises medical and student AI apps, with few concrete harms named.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI leadership will determine future warfare, cybersecurity and "unwavering economic influence," and calls it "the future for our country." That implies large transformation, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns center on national-security threats, including cyber threats, adversary exploitation of AI, and data theft. He also mentions harm to vulnerable people. He does not discuss loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: The China race is the dominant lens across most of his statements. He says it is "not one the United States can afford to lose" and that "we have to win." He pairs this with calls for light regulation and a moratorium on state laws, but the race is clearly primary.
just.regulation: He opposes a "heavy-handed regulatory regime" and prefers industry self-regulation unless it fails. He also favors a moratorium (apparently on state laws) and is worried about slowing innovation. He allows some federal standards and guidelines to protect vulnerable people.

members.summary: Darin LaHood talks about AI mainly as a strategic competition with China. He stresses American leadership, export controls on chips, and countering the CCP, as with DeepSeek and the Chip Security Act. He sees AI as promising but perilous, prefers industry self-regulation and light federal standards, and supports a moratorium. He also highlights beneficial uses such as medical AI and student apps.

members.name: Warren Davidson

just.ai_overall: He calls AI "one of the most important technologies of our time" and wants to use it to solve problems. He also warns repeatedly about surveillance, data exploitation, and AI as a "freight train", so promise and risk are roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as a "freight train in everyone's life" and one of the most important technologies of our time, and expects it to change work and productivity. None of the statements mention AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: He raises a large-scale cyber scenario in which AI breaks bank-level encryption and the banks would have to be shut down. His other concerns are surveillance and privacy, and he never raises loss of control. The "existential threat" remark (s18) does not clearly refer to AI.
just.china_race: He says the U.S. is in a global AI race and wants to win it, but also that beating China doesn't mean becoming like China. The race appears alongside privacy, child safety, and civil liberties concerns and is not the dominant lens.
just.regulation: He wants specific safeguards, privacy and data-property rules, and a durable federal framework that preempts harmful state laws while protecting child safety, fraud, and IP. He opposes slipping AI preemption or immunity into must-pass bills, and he says it is "way early" to regulate AI. That adds up to targeted rules and not a broad regulatory regime.

members.summary: Warren Davidson describes AI as an important and powerful technology that needs guardrails, and he often argues that privacy is the "base layer for ethical AI." He strongly opposed the AI preemption/"amnesty" provision in the 2025 reconciliation bill, mainly on process grounds, and wants a standalone, debated AI bill. He backs U.S. leadership against China and a federal framework, while stressing surveillance, data rights, and the limits of Congress's ability to keep pace with the technology.

members.name: James Comer

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as an opportunity for efficiency, fraud detection, innovation and defense, and says it should be unleashed responsibly. He raises some concerns, such as surveillance pricing and privacy, but they read as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI 'the next frontier' and a 'transformative technology', which suggests large change. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises are everyday ones: privacy, civil rights, surveillance pricing, and companies avoiding responsibility. None are catastrophic or about loss of control.
just.china_race: He says the US leads in AI and must keep its edge, and that data centers will otherwise be built in China. Competition is a recurring theme but sits alongside other concerns such as local control, privacy and responsible use.
just.regulation: He wants 'smart guardrails' but opposes heavy-handed rules, new agencies and bureaucracies. He is wary of broad regulation and supports targeted transparency measures.

members.summary: Comer speaks about AI mostly as an opportunity, especially for government efficiency, rooting out fraud, defense and innovation. He stresses keeping the US ahead of China and backs 'smart' guardrails, but he opposes heavy-handed regulation and new federal agencies. His concerns are about privacy, civil liberties, surveillance pricing and regulatory capture, not catastrophic risk.

members.name: Dwight Evans

just.ai_overall: Both statements frame AI only as a vehicle for harm: disinformation aimed at Black voters and a racist AI video. Neither mentions benefits, so the lean is concerned, though the evidence is thin.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement addresses AGI, transformative change, or the future capabilities of AI.
just.x_risk: The only risks raised are everyday harms: disinformation, voter suppression, and racist content. None is framed as catastrophic.
just.china_race: China and any AI race are never mentioned.
just.regulation: He calls for vigilance against AI disinformation but proposes no rules, laws, or regulatory stance.

members.summary: Dwight Evans mentions AI only in passing, as a source of harm. He links AI disinformation to efforts to disenfranchise Black voters and criticizes a racist AI video posted by the president. The statements offer no views on AI policy, the technology's future, or competition with China.

members.name: John Kennedy

just.ai_overall: He says AI can make lives better, but he pairs that with warnings that it could take jobs or kill us, and he criticizes data center costs and AI hype. Promise and risk appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: He describes recursive self-improvement producing an independent species that humans cannot control, and says even a 1% chance deserves serious attention. That treats advanced, human-surpassing AI as a real possibility, though he gives no explicit timeline. He also calls productivity claims hype.
just.x_risk: He repeatedly raises AI killing us or escaping human control, including a 'berserk wing' that could kill everyone, and he introduced a kill-switch bill. He treats this as serious enough to legislate.
just.china_race: China appears only in a question about Nvidia chip export limits and in one post about China's AI progress and CHIPS Act spending. It is not a recurring lens for his AI policy.
just.regulation: He backs mandatory AI-content disclosure, a financial fraud bill, and a kill-switch requirement for advanced models. He also says existing law is insufficient and that safeguards and accountability do not conflict with innovation. He wants companies to run the kill switch rather than the government, and he rejects new government committees, but the rules are still substantial.

members.summary: Kennedy describes AI as something that could improve lives but also take jobs or 'kill us all.' Since 2026 he has focused on loss-of-control scenarios such as recursive self-improvement and has introduced a kill-switch bill, which he says should be run by companies and not the government. He also backs AI-content disclosure and anti-fraud rules, criticizes data centers' water, energy, and subsidy demands, and mocks AI developers and productivity hype.

members.name: Margaret Wood Hassan

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's potential (health, government services, 'maximize the potential of AI') with serious safety, security, and scam risks. The balance is close to even, though most of her statements focus on risks.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is advancing rapidly, but no statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation on the scale of the internet.
just.x_risk: She flags catastrophic misuse such as bioweapons and AI behaving unpredictably against designers' intent. She also works on research so AI cannot 'easily behave in unexpected ways'. That treats loss of control as a real concern, though she never uses existential-risk framing.
just.china_race: China appears as a recurring concern: export controls, Chinese surveillance AI, and adversaries misusing AI. She also stresses keeping US leadership 'while protecting public safety'. It is balanced with safety themes and is not the dominant lens.
just.regulation: She backs substantial oversight, including a FedRAMP-like safety evaluation program for AI, 'balanced oversight of the most advanced AI models', and safety research frameworks. She also backs targeted deepfake and scam measures. She does not call for licensing or pauses.

members.summary: Hassan treats AI as a technology with real promise, especially in health care and government services, but most of her statements focus on safety and security risks. She stresses scams, deepfakes, kids' privacy, and national-security threats such as bioweapons and unpredictable AI behavior. She favors bipartisan, balanced oversight of advanced models and safety research while keeping US leadership against China.

members.name: Catherine Cortez Masto

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's potential and innovation with real threats, such as cybercrime, terrorism, discrimination, and worker harms, and says guardrails are needed. The balance is fairly even, with a safety-focused tilt in her 2026 statements.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI has the potential to profoundly change many aspects of life and that capabilities are growing by the minute. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: She flags large-scale misuse such as terrorism, cybercrime, and national-security threats from AI and chips in adversaries' hands. She does not mention loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: Staying ahead of China recurs in her statements, including export controls and the 'AI race'. It is balanced against safety guardrails and global standards rather than used to oppose regulation.
just.regulation: She calls for AI safety hearings, global safety and transparency standards, safeguards, and worker protections. She has also backed targeted bills on deepfakes and housing bias. She does not call for licensing or a new agency, and the broader safety framework goes beyond purely targeted rules.

members.summary: Cortez Masto describes AI as a technology with real promise and growing risks, and she stresses protecting families, workers, and national security. She has backed targeted measures on deepfakes and algorithmic housing bias, and in 2026 she called for AI safety hearings and global standards. She frames competition with China as important, especially through chip export controls, but pairs it with guardrails and criticizes the Trump administration for inaction.

members.name: Bradley Scott Schneider

just.ai_overall: He calls AI both a great opportunity for human advancement and a threat to humanity itself. He gives the two roughly equal weight and stresses the need for oversight.
just.agi_pilled: He says frontier models are increasingly gaining the ability to break out and act on their own, and he describes AI as a potential threat to humanity. This treats highly capable, autonomous advanced AI as a real near-term concern, though he never uses the terms AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He says AI is a threat to humanity itself and compares it to nuclear fission's potential to wipe out life as we know it. He also worries about systems breaking out of human control and wants international guardrails like nonproliferation, which makes this a top-tier concern.
just.china_race: China appears only once, in a line that the U.S. can compete with China while protecting safety. Race framing is not a driving lens for him.
just.regulation: He wants testing, oversight, safeguards, incident reporting, and meaningful scrutiny of the most powerful frontier systems, plus international guardrails. This is substantial regulation of frontier AI, though he stops short of explicitly calling for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Schneider describes AI as both a major opportunity and a possible threat to humanity. He focuses on frontier models that could act autonomously, and he compares the situation to nuclear technology. He supports testing, oversight, and international guardrails for the most powerful systems, and says the U.S. can compete with China while protecting safety.

members.name: Andy Biggs

just.ai_overall: He praises AI as a tool for efficiency, savings and growth (s1, s2, s3). He also repeatedly raises criminal exploitation, deepfakes, child abuse material and national security threats (s5, s7, s9). Promise and risk both feature, roughly in balance.
just.agi_pilled: In a hearing he said artificial superintelligence may arrive before 2030 instead of 2050, and that algorithms may eventually act as first movers. He treats this as a real near-term possibility, though he raises it only briefly.
just.x_risk: He raises AI combined with drones as an exponentially growing national security threat, and AI-enabled criminal exploitation at scale (s4, s9). He does not discuss loss of control or extinction risk.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He backs targeted rules on AI-generated CSAM, deepfakes, victim remedies and age verification for AI sexual content (s5, s6, s8, s15). He also pushes to reduce general federal overregulation (s1, s2). That fits a targeted approach, not broad frameworks.

members.summary: Biggs mostly talks about AI as a tool for government efficiency and deregulation, and as a source of criminal exploitation, deepfakes and child sexual abuse material. He chaired a hearing on AI and crime, and said in it that superintelligence could arrive before 2030. He supports narrow legal fixes and wants to protect Arizona ratepayers from data center costs, but does not call for broad AI regulation.

members.name: Ro Khanna

just.ai_overall: He credits AI with real benefits (medicine, advanced manufacturing, productivity, small business) and says he is neither a doomer nor an accelerationist. Most of his statements focus on job displacement, billionaire control and catastrophic risk, so the two sides are roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He treats loss of control, recursive self-improvement and human extinction from advanced AI as real near-term concerns, and has asked witnesses about AGI timelines. He does not give explicit short timelines, so this stops short of 4.
just.x_risk: He cites a 10% extinction estimate, warns of a 'civilizational extinction risk', and calls for a pause on recursive self-improvement. He compares AI governance to nuclear power and a 'nuclear war', and makes the risk a central part of his current agenda.
just.china_race: He wants the U.S. to stay ahead of China on AI and supports chip export controls. He also pushes a verifiable AI safety treaty and standards with China, so race framing is balanced by cooperation and does not override other concerns.
just.regulation: He calls for a new federal AI agency modeled on nuclear and aviation oversight. He also wants pre-certification, mandatory third-party verification, civil and criminal liability, a pause on recursive self-improvement, and opposes preemption of state AI laws.

members.summary: Ro Khanna frames AI mainly as a question of who controls it. He argues for a worker-first agenda that includes taxing automation, jobs programs and limits on displacement, and he is highly critical of tech billionaires. His later statements stress catastrophic and loss-of-control risk and call for a federal AI agency, liability and an international safety agreement with China. He also acknowledges AI's benefits and supports AI education and manufacturing, and he says he is neither a doomer nor an accelerationist.

members.name: Jimmy Panetta

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs AI's potential (economic growth, security tools, local innovation) with serious threats and calls for guardrails. Recent statements lean toward concern about safety, but he still stresses benefits, so the overall view is balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is reshaping the economy, workforce and education, and that it is central to modern warfare. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence, so this stays at transformative without AGI.
just.x_risk: He warns that rapid AI adoption without greater safety controls and slower development could produce incidents that threaten security and safety, and he cites AI companies' own warnings about dangers. He frames this as protecting 'our country and humanity,' but he does not explicitly discuss loss of control or extinction. His concerns also include cyber and national-security risks.
just.china_race: He recurs to staying competitive with China and keeping a technological edge, and he cites this in the context of security. He balances it with calls for global standards, testing and coordination, and for guardrails. He does not use the race to argue against regulation.
just.regulation: He backs enforceable safeguards, safety standards, transparency, testing and reporting, and a broad federal framework. He criticizes the lack of federal action and wants Congress to vote on AI safeguards. This is substantial regulation, short of licensing or a pause.

members.summary: Panetta describes AI as a technology with significant potential for the economy, security and local innovation, and he regularly highlights AI-powered projects in his district. Since 2026 his statements have focused more on serious risks, and he calls for enforceable guardrails, safety testing and a federal framework, while criticizing Republican leaders for inaction. He frames US competitiveness, especially with China, as important, but he pairs it with calls for international standards and coordination.

members.name: Salud O. Carbajal

just.ai_overall: He is enthusiastic about AI research and its practical uses (the UCSB institute, protein design for sustainable products) and describes AI as part of a coming technological revolution. He objects to deceptive AI-generated campaign content, but that concern is narrow and does not outweigh the optimism.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is part of a new technological and industrial revolution that will completely change daily life, which fits the 'very transformative' level. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: The only risks he raises are everyday harms: disinformation and deceptive or racist AI-generated campaign content. He gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He condemns deceptive AI-generated political ads, but he does not endorse any rule, law, or regulatory approach for AI.

members.summary: Carbajal speaks about AI mostly as a promising area for research and local economic pride, praising UCSB's AI institute and an NSF-funded protein design project. He calls AI part of a new technological and industrial revolution. His critical remarks are limited to condemning deceptive or racist AI-generated political ads, and he does not discuss policy, China, or catastrophic risks.

members.name: Nanette Diaz Barragán

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's benefits (health care, translation, helping small businesses, access to tools like Google) with concerns about errors, bias, disinformation, and job loss. The two sides appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements mention AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's long-term transformation. A passing line about 'rapidly changing digital landscape' is too thin to score.
just.x_risk: Her stated risks are everyday harms: translation errors, bias, election disinformation, job loss, and electricity costs. She gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. The only competition language is a generic 'America can lead in AI and innovation, but it must do so safely.'
just.regulation: She says Congress needs to regulate AI, objects to a 10-year state-law moratorium, and worries about an unchecked industry. She also backs consumer transparency legislation and making data centers cover their power costs. These go beyond narrow fixes, but she does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Barragán talks about AI as a useful tool, especially in health care, translation, and for small businesses, but one that needs guardrails. Her concerns are practical: bias against Latino and underserved communities, translation errors, election disinformation, worker protections, and data center electricity costs. She supports regulation and opposes preempting state AI laws, and she does not discuss AGI, existential risk, or competition with China.

members.name: J. Luis Correa

just.ai_overall: He speaks about AI almost entirely as an opportunity, encouraging people to explore it and praising its uses in education, accessibility and border security. He mentions civil liberties protections only briefly and does not dwell on risks.
just.agi_pilled: No statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation. His AI remarks are about specific applications and student projects, which is not enough to place him on this scale.
just.x_risk: He never discusses catastrophic or existential AI risk. His only harm-related statement concerns nonconsensual deepfake images, and a single everyday-harm statement is too thin to score as 1.
just.china_race: China appears once, in a remark about Chinese power-plant building and AI adoption by Chinese small businesses. That suggests some attention to competition, but there is no explicit race framing or policy argument to score.
just.regulation: He backed targeted legislation on nonconsensual intimate images, including deepfakes, and wants AI in homeland security used with civil rights protections. He shows no support for broad AI regulatory frameworks.

members.summary: Correa talks about AI in an upbeat, practical way, highlighting student app and robotics projects, border-security technology, and encouraging people not to fear it. His one clear policy concern is protecting victims of nonconsensual deepfake images, and he supported bipartisan legislation on it. He briefly points to China's AI adoption, but he does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Lisa Blunt Rochester

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs 'incredible opportunities' with 'unique challenges.' Her tone has grown more alarmed in 2026 ('AI is out of control'), but she still names real benefits, so the balance reads as mixed.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is disrupting the economy and the workforce and that its capabilities are growing quickly. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence, and the Star Trek/Terminator remark only describes what others fear.
just.x_risk: She says that even a 1% chance of AI wiping out human life warrants slowing down for safeguards. She also raises 'autonomous hackings' and AI systems accessing networks without authorization, which points toward loss-of-control concerns, though she does not make existential risk her main theme.
just.china_race: She says the US 'cannot afford to lose the global AI race' and wants to win it. She balances this with environmental, security and safety concerns, and later criticizes an 'out of control' race.
just.regulation: She backs state and congressional authority to regulate and demands accountability and safeguards from frontier AI companies. She also pushes for hearings with AI CEOs and for transparency measures. Her stated proposals are mostly targeted (literacy, fraud, data-center transparency), so she stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Blunt Rochester describes AI as offering real opportunities in health, the economy and education, while stressing workforce disruption, safety and data-center impacts. Her 2026 statements are much more alarmed, calling AI 'out of control,' citing autonomous hacking incidents, and warning of even a 1% chance of human extinction. She backs winning the AI race against competitors but favors congressional oversight, accountability for AI companies, AI literacy and targeted bills such as one on fraud.

members.name: Neal P. Dunn

just.ai_overall: He calls AI exciting and revolutionary, especially in health care, and wants to harness its full potential. He also flags misuse, deepfakes, fraud, and a disturbing loss-of-control scenario, but treats these as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He mentions 'the AGI world' only in a question to a witness and says AI is 'revolutionizing healthcare.' Neither shows his own expectation of AGI or transformative change.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security, cyber-warfare, and biowarfare-related threats and misuse by bad actors. He also voiced concern about an AI blackmail experiment ('my computer could turn on me'), but this was a passing reaction and not a sustained loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: Competition with China recurs across his statements: maintaining a competitive edge, countering the CCP, 'securing American dominance,' and noting that China moves fast with no regulations. He pairs this with other concerns such as fraud and deepfakes, but the race is a primary lens.
just.regulation: He explicitly says the US 'must have a light touch on AI regulations' and praises a pro-innovation approach. He also backs narrow measures on deepfake labeling and AI fraud penalties, which pulls him slightly above the lowest level.

members.summary: Dunn presents AI as an exciting innovation, with particular enthusiasm for health care. He frames policy around staying ahead of China and protecting national security. He backs narrow measures against deepfakes and AI-enabled fraud while saying the US should take a light-touch approach to regulation. He expressed concern about an AI blackmail experiment, but otherwise rarely discusses catastrophic risk or AGI in his own words.

members.name: Darren Soto

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly calls AI 'awe-inspiring' and 'incredible', and stresses its economic and health benefits and its role in U.S. leadership. He pairs this with worries about disruption, chatbot harms to kids, and deepfakes, but treats those as manageable with guardrails.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as becoming a bigger part of daily life and as 'transforming the future of healthcare'. He is clearly expecting broad economic change, but never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: chatbot harms to kids, deepfakes, robocalls, fraud, job disruption, and higher utility costs. None of them are catastrophic or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: Only one statement frames AI as a race, saying 'America must continue to lead in the AI race. Otherwise, our rivals will fill that void', and China is never named. Other statements stress U.S. leadership in general terms, and the race is not a main lens for him.
just.regulation: He supports targeted rules: the AI Accountability Act on harmful impersonation, limits on kids' access to chatbots, disclosure and 'rules of the road', election and robocall protections, and privacy law. He also criticizes efforts to ban AI protections and says states play a role. He wants thoughtful regulation but not broad licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Darren Soto talks about AI mostly as an economic and innovation opportunity, citing Central Florida healthcare, simulation, chip manufacturing and consumer-safety uses. He pairs this with concern about everyday harms such as chatbots and kids, deepfakes, robocalls, job disruption, and data-center energy costs. He backs targeted guardrails and bipartisan bills, and does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Brian J. Mast

just.ai_overall: He calls AI 'the future,' praises AI infrastructure investment, and promotes AI training. His concerns focus mainly on adversaries getting advanced chips, not on AI harms, so he reads as mostly optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI and other technologies will determine economic and military power for generations, and that AI dominance will decide who strikes first. That is transformative framing, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He raises national-security risks such as AI-enabled military advantage and AI-powered drones, framed as adversary misuse and warfare. He never discusses loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: The AI race with the CCP is his dominant lens: he calls it the most critical national security threat, chairs hearings on it, and sponsors chip-export bills. He argues 'we cannot win if we keep handing our advantages' to China.
just.regulation: He backs specific, targeted measures such as the AI OVERWATCH Act and chip export controls, but these are national-security rules, not broad AI regulation. He also voices skepticism about Congress's regulatory record.

members.summary: Mast talks about AI almost entirely through national security and competition with China. He is optimistic about AI's economic and educational potential. His main policy work is legislation and public pressure to keep advanced AI chips from China's military, including a public fight with Nvidia's CEO. He says little about domestic AI safety, loss of control, or broad regulation.

members.name: Raja Krishnamoorthi

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs AI's promise (scientific breakthroughs, medical advances, 'defining technology') with serious dangers (deepfakes, loss of control, surveillance), and he frames both as needing guardrails. The balance is roughly even.
just.agi_pilled: He discusses AGI directly in a hearing, citing AGI safety, self-improving systems, and 'superintelligence'. He treats AGI as a near-term prospect that needs a safety bill, but he does not give explicit short timelines.
just.x_risk: He raises rogue AI, loss of human control, and self-improving systems, and he cites Hinton's 10–20% extinction estimate. He also lists nuclear command and bio risks, and he is sponsoring an AGI Safety Act. He does not clearly rank extinction risk as his top priority, so this stops short of a 4.
just.china_race: China competition is a very frequent lens in his AI statements, covering chip export controls, DeepSeek, CCP surveillance, and 'how America wins' the AI race. He does not say the race overrides regulation. He pairs it with safety and oversight, and he also supports US-China talks on AI risk.
just.regulation: He supports substantial rules: independent inspection and validation of frontier models, government oversight during development, enforceable safeguards, and an AGI Safety Act. He also opposes self-policing and federal preemption of state laws. He stops short of calling for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Krishnamoorthi describes AI as a defining technology with real benefits in medicine, science, and the economy. He also stresses dangers: deepfakes and election disinformation, foreign adversary use, chatbot harms to kids, and loss of control over advanced AI. He frames much of his AI policy around competition with the CCP, with chip export controls and bans on adversary models, and he supports enforceable oversight of frontier AI over industry self-regulation.

members.name: Jim Banks

just.ai_overall: He sees real promise (productivity, a better economy, military edge) alongside serious risks (job losses, weaponization, loss of control, a need for oversight). Neither side clearly dominates.
just.agi_pilled: He compares AI to atomic weapons as a paradigm shift and discusses artificial superintelligence as something companies are actively pursuing. He treats it as a real concern, but gives no explicit timelines.
just.x_risk: He raises unresolved questions about whether powerful AI can be kept under human control, especially with superintelligence. He also warns about models building WMDs or taking over systems autonomously, so loss of control is treated as real. He does not frame it as the top priority.
just.china_race: Beating the CCP in an AI race is a primary lens across many statements, including chips, military superiority, and a 'moral race.' He also supports oversight and worker protections, so the race does not override every other concern.
just.regulation: He calls for more federal oversight of frontier models, including internal and undisclosed ones, and for national security testing against WMD and autonomy risks. He also backs export controls on chips and measures against insider threats.

members.summary: Banks frames AI mainly through competition with China and national security, and he pushes export controls on advanced chips. He also acknowledges job disruption and calls for federal oversight of frontier models. In 2026 statements he raises loss-of-control concerns and superintelligence, while still expecting AI to improve the economy.

members.name: Roger Marshall

just.ai_overall: He stresses AI's benefits for health care, workers, and the economy, and uses it heavily himself. His concerns (bioterrorism, data center costs, privacy, kids) are treated as manageable with guardrails.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is 'transforming our economy and the future of work' and calls it the 'AI era,' which suggests large-scale change. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He names AI-enabled bioterrorism and novel pathogens or bioweapons as his biggest concern, which is a large-scale misuse risk. He does not discuss loss of control.
just.china_race: He says national security comes first and that China cannot get ahead of the U.S. military. China is not a recurring theme across his other AI statements, and he balances it with transparency, kids, and privacy.
just.regulation: He explicitly favors a 'light touch' approach and warns against destroying innovation. He still backs targeted guardrails on transparency, child protection, and privacy, and supports local data center moratoriums.

members.summary: Marshall, a physician, talks about AI mainly as a practical tool for health care, workers, and rural communities, and he says he uses it for hours each day. He supports a 'light touch' federal approach built on transparency, child protection, and privacy, and frames AI through national security and competition with China. His main catastrophic worry is AI-enabled bioterrorism. He is also skeptical of data centers, citing utility costs, water, and tax breaks.

members.name: Clay Higgins

just.ai_overall: He calls AI an 'Armageddon level threat' and a tool of government weaponization, with only brief acknowledgments that it can be powerful or serve mankind. Harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or economy-wide transformation. His comments concern government use of AI and rapid deployment, not expectations of radical capability.
just.x_risk: He uses 'Armageddon level threat' language, but the concern is government misuse of AI to enforce laws and control citizens, not loss of control of advanced AI. The framing is catastrophic but about misuse and authoritarian abuse. The hyperbole is not tied to a specific large-scale scenario like bioweapons.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He backs targeted measures: a bill banning federal use of AI for law enforcement, and legislation protecting constituent communications from automated bad-actor content. He says AI 'should be effectively controlled' but does not propose a broad framework for AI companies.

members.summary: Higgins mostly frames AI as a threat, especially as a tool for the federal government to surveil, enforce rules against, and control Americans, and he has called it an 'Armageddon level threat.' He acknowledges AI can be powerful and beneficial but stresses individual rights and human control. His policy focus is narrow: barring federal use of AI for enforcement and protecting constituent input from automated content. He also asks about data center energy use and occasionally jokes about AI.

members.name: Mike Johnson

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as an innovation and national-competitiveness opportunity that government should not smother. He also acknowledges peril to creators and says models must be safe, and urges against panic, so risks read as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI could 'revolutionize a range of industries', 'change our lives', and 'transform the world as we know it', which is transformative language. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday or policy-level: copyright, deepfakes, model safety, energy costs, and China's misuse for espionage and election interference. He raises no loss-of-control or existential framing.
just.china_race: The China race is a dominant, recurring lens, and he uses it explicitly to argue against moratoria, emergency legislation, and 'hyper-regulation'. He says overregulating would cause the US to 'lose the race to China'.
just.regulation: He opposes moratoria and hyper-regulation, favors industry self-regulation and voluntary steps, and wants to 'regulate only where we must'. He also backs a single national framework that preempts state patchworks, with some child-protection and creator provisions.

members.summary: Johnson talks about AI chiefly as an engine of innovation and a national-security contest with China. He repeatedly rejects a moratorium, emergency legislation, and state-by-state rules, and favors self-regulation and a single light national framework. He also says companies must make safe models, and in earlier committee remarks he raised copyright and deepfake concerns.

members.name: Jamie Raskin

just.ai_overall: He calls AI a revolutionary technology that will remake society and says it can improve public functions. He pairs that with sustained concern about surveillance, concentration of power, and misuse, so his stance is balanced, perhaps leaning cautious.
just.agi_pilled: He compares AI to the telephone, computer, and Internet and says it will remake society, commerce, and government, which is transformative. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are mostly everyday harms such as surveillance, privacy, data misuse, and bad chatbot advice. The 'human-species security problem' quote hints at larger stakes but does not develop a loss-of-control or catastrophic argument.
just.china_race: China appears mainly in the context of protecting trade secrets and cybersecurity and scrutinizing economic espionage. He treats the 'arms race' as someone else's phrase and does not make winning a primary lens.
just.regulation: He backs substantial guardrails, including transparency and safety testing for high-stakes systems, standards of care for AI platforms, and the Biden executive order. He opposes a moratorium that would preempt state laws, though he is open to a national law that works.

members.summary: Raskin describes AI as a revolutionary technology that will remake society and the economy, and he focuses on civil liberties, surveillance, market concentration, and accountability. He strongly opposes a federal moratorium on state AI laws and favors transparency, safety testing, and oversight, including restoring stronger federal guardrails. He frequently criticizes Elon Musk's AI use and raises copyright and national security issues, but he rarely discusses AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Jack Bergman

just.ai_overall: The statements address the local impacts of data centers and a question about military AI ethics. None states an overall view of AI as promising or threatening.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements mentions AGI, superintelligence, or transformative change from AI.
just.x_risk: The only risk-related remark is a question about ethical and moral implications of AI in the Defense Department. It does not frame catastrophic or existential risk and does not reject it.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned in the statements.
just.regulation: He supports a one-year moratorium on new AI data centers in Michigan, local regulatory authority, and a rule that data centers pay their own energy costs. These are targeted, infrastructure-focused measures rather than a broad framework for AI models, and they are mostly about siting and ratepayers.

members.summary: Bergman's statements focus on the local and energy effects of AI data centers. He backs a temporary state moratorium on new data centers, local control over siting, and making data centers pay their own way so families don't face higher utility bills. In a 2023 hearing he also asked who is responsible for the ethical and moral implications of AI in the Defense Department. He says little about AI's broader promise, risks, AGI, or China.

members.name: Ted Budd

just.ai_overall: He calls himself on the optimistic side, says AI will enhance Americans' capabilities, and says humans will collaborate with AI instead of being replaced. He does acknowledge public worries about jobs and kids, but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He expects AI to change how jobs are done and frames AI as an economy-wide competition. He mentions AGI only once, in a question about China unlocking it first, and does not state his own timeline or expectation.
just.x_risk: He flags AI-generated biological or chemical weapons as a real prospect and sponsored a bill on public health preparedness for AI threats. He does not discuss loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: Winning the AI race against China is a recurring and primary lens for him. He applies it to energy, permitting, exports of the US tech stack, and values. He does not use it to reject all constraints, and he also raises other concerns, which keeps it below 4.
just.regulation: He urges the federal government to tread carefully on new regulation. He favors removing roadblocks, giving regulatory certainty, and a regulatory sandbox, and he worries that US regulation could let China get ahead. He has not supported broad rules.

members.summary: Budd speaks about AI mainly as an economic and national-security opportunity. He is optimistic that AI will augment workers, and he stresses winning the AI race against China through energy, permitting reform, and exporting the US tech stack. He favors light-touch, innovation-friendly rules such as a sandbox and cautions against new regulation. He acknowledges public worries about jobs and kids, and he has flagged AI-enabled bio and chemical threats.

members.name: Don Bacon

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as a strategic and economic opportunity. He urges leaning into it, dismisses 'Luddites,' and pushes faster adoption, while acknowledging some risks such as terrorist exploitation of jailbroken AI and the need for guardrails if warranted.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is changing the world and reshaping the cyber domain and warfare, and he groups it with quantum as decisive for national power. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns center on national-security misuse, such as terrorists exploiting jailbroken AI, AI-enabled cyber operations, and AI threats to nuclear command and control. He does not discuss loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: The AI race with China is his dominant frame. He says 'coming in second in AI is coming in last,' argues that opposing data centers or over-regulating helps China, and wants chip export limits.
just.regulation: He warns that over-regulation will lose the AI race and supports a single federal standard over 50 state standards. He allows that guardrails may be needed later and backs narrow measures, such as excluding adversary AI firms from DoD and holding platforms accountable for antisemitism.

members.summary: Bacon, who chairs the House Armed Services cyber and AI subcommittee, talks about AI mostly as a national-security and economic competition with China. He is strongly pro-adoption and pro-data-center, argues against over-regulation and a state-by-state patchwork, and says guardrails could come later if warranted. His risk talk is about misuse, such as terrorists and cyber operations, not existential danger.

members.name: Josh Gottheimer

just.ai_overall: He consistently pairs AI's promise (health, science, economy) with serious security and consumer risks. He says AI has 'massive benefits' but is also a 'five-alarm' risk that needs mandatory guardrails. The two sides are roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as advancing at 'lightning speed', 'changing everything', and able to 'transform our economy', which suggests major societal change. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: He repeatedly warns of rogue AI agents 'escaping containment' and stresses 'keeping humans in control' and being able to 'shut it down if it goes rogue'. He also flags bioweapon and grid-attack risks. He stops short of extinction framing or comparisons to nuclear war.
just.china_race: He repeatedly calls the situation an 'AI Cold War' with China that the US must win, and the framing recurs across dozens of statements. He qualifies it with 'win the right way' and pairs it with mandatory testing, so it does not override his support for constraints.
just.regulation: He backs mandatory pre-deployment testing and a shot-clocked government review of frontier models, and rejects voluntary standards and third-party audits. He also supports specific rules on labeling, agent identification, and kids' safety. He rejects pausing AI and does not call for a licensing agency.

members.summary: Gottheimer, Co-Chair of the House AI Commission, describes AI as a major opportunity in health, science, and the economy. He puts heavy emphasis on national security, cyber, bio, and rogue-agent risks. He frames AI as a Cold War-style race with China that the US must win 'the right way', and he backs mandatory pre-deployment government review of frontier models and a range of bipartisan bills, while opposing a pause or a halt to innovation.

members.name: Jacky Rosen

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs enthusiasm for AI's potential (scientific breakthroughs, cyber defense, a personal programming background) with serious concerns about security, scams, hate speech, and catastrophic damage. The balance is roughly even, with a call for guardrails.
just.agi_pilled: She describes AI as rapidly changing the technology landscape and the world, and as a 'powerful technology', but never mentions AGI or superintelligence. This suggests a view of AI as very transformative without explicit AGI expectations.
just.x_risk: She says the AI industry itself calls the technology a threat to humanity, and that AI could cause 'catastrophic damages' without guardrails. She also raises concern about AI evading safety mechanisms and about keeping humans in the loop. She does not use explicit extinction or top-priority framing.
just.china_race: China competition recurs across her statements: staying ahead of China, banning DeepSeek, and chip export controls. She says the US must 'continue to lead, particularly outcompeting China', but she pairs this with guardrails rather than using it to argue against regulation.
just.regulation: She calls for guardrails and safety mechanisms, congressional hearings with AI executives, and responsible rules on practices like surveillance pricing. She also supports privacy regulation and benchmarks. This goes beyond narrow fixes but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Rosen, a former computer programmer, talks about AI as a technology with extraordinary promise for science, cyber defense, and public safety, and she backs AI workforce and infrastructure investment. She focuses heavily on national security, cyber threats, and Chinese AI such as DeepSeek, and sponsors bipartisan bills on these. Her later statements turn more alarmed, citing industry warnings of a threat to humanity, antisemitism in chatbots, and surveillance pricing, and she calls for guardrails and hearings with AI executives.

members.name: Adriano Espaillat

just.ai_overall: He pairs optimism about AI's promise ('potential to revolutionize our society', 'harness its benefits') with serious concerns about elections, bias, workers and energy costs. The balance is roughly even, with an emphasis on responsible and equitable development.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI 'has the potential to revolutionize our society' and 'is NOW,' and he links it to the 'economy of tomorrow.' This suggests large-scale transformation, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: election deepfakes, misinformation, bias, workforce effects and energy bills. Phrases like 'before it's too late' are about democracy and elections, not catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He introduced election-focused AI legislation and says 'we must govern and regulate AI.' He also criticizes Congress for not regulating automated systems, praises the executive order on safety and accountability, and wants safeguards for workers and consumers. This goes beyond a single targeted fix, though he proposes no frontier-model licensing regime or new agency.

members.summary: Espaillat talks about AI mainly through election deepfakes, equity and bias, and AI literacy for Latino and underserved communities. He sees AI's promise but stresses responsible, inclusive development and says Congress should regulate it, starting with his Candidate Voice Fraud Prohibition Act. He does not discuss AGI, existential risk or China, and he briefly links AI data centers to higher energy bills.

members.name: Brian K. Fitzpatrick

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as offering 'enormous opportunity and equally serious questions' and calls for embracing innovation without abandoning responsibility. He also welcomes AI investment, while stressing national security risks, worker protection, and deepfakes.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI-related projects 'transformative' and says AI is 'reshaping the future of work' and that 'rules governing advanced AI are being written now'. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security risks such as threats to critical infrastructure, AI-enabled cyber aggression, and an AI-run Chinese espionage operation. He does not discuss loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: He repeatedly frames AI policy around staying ahead of adversaries and leading global standards, and cites a Chinese state-sponsored AI cyber operation. He pairs this with safety and worker concerns and does not use the race to argue against rules.
just.regulation: He pushes dozens of bipartisan bills on AI security, transparency, and independent oversight. He also backs an international framework with testing and incident reporting, and the deepfake and election-AI bills. This goes beyond narrow targeted rules, though it stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Fitzpatrick talks about AI as both an opportunity and a risk. He welcomes AI investment and data centers in his district, and he stresses worker protections, deepfake and election safeguards, and national security. He frames US leadership against China and other adversaries as important, and he supports bipartisan bills for AI security, transparency, testing, and oversight. He does not discuss AGI or existential risk.

members.name: Lloyd Smucker

just.ai_overall: He says America should lead the world in AI and favors letting the market develop it, which points to an opportunity framing. His concerns, mainly energy costs for ratepayers, are narrow and manageable, though the evidence is thin.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements mention AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's transformative effects.
just.x_risk: No statement discusses catastrophic, existential, or loss-of-control risks. His only stated concern is data center energy costs.
just.china_race: China is never mentioned. 'Lead the world in AI' is a general competitiveness statement, not a race framing against China.
just.regulation: He says government bureaucrats setting AI rules would be the worst thing, wants the market to develop it, and objects to a 50-state patchwork. That fits the anti-regulation, preemption-leaning end, though he backs a narrow ratepayer bill on data center costs.

members.summary: Smucker presents AI as something America should lead in. He is wary of government-set rules, preferring that the market shape AI, and he objects to a patchwork of state regulations. His one concrete policy interest is the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would make data centers pay for their own energy infrastructure rather than shifting costs to families and small businesses.

members.name: David Kustoff

just.ai_overall: He celebrates AI investment and student AI projects as economic and innovation opportunities. He also names AI-enabled robocall scams as a harm, but the tone is mostly optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI the 'next generation of technology' and a driver of an innovation hub, but never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or society-wide transformation.
just.x_risk: The only risks he raises are everyday harms like AI voice-mimicking scam robocalls and spoofing. He frames none of them as catastrophic.
just.china_race: He praises the AI Action Plan for 'U.S. dominance' in a list of administration wins, but he never frames AI policy around China or a race with it.
just.regulation: He backs narrow measures against AI-enabled robocall fraud, such as the DO NOT Call Act's higher penalties and the bipartisan bill giving prosecutors more power. He expresses no support for broad AI frameworks.

members.summary: Kustoff mostly talks about AI as an economic development opportunity, especially xAI's Colossus supercomputer investment in Memphis, and he praises student AI work. His one concern is AI-enabled robocall scams, which he addresses with targeted legislation that raises penalties. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or broad AI regulation, and he mentions the AI race only in passing.

members.name: Vicente Gonzalez

just.ai_overall: He cites AI's potential economic gains and sees it as a source of new industry, but he also raises scams that target seniors. The evidence is thin, but it points to a mixed view.
just.agi_pilled: He never mentions AGI or superintelligence. The only large-scale claim is a quoted GDP estimate, which is not enough to show he expects transformative change.
just.x_risk: His only stated AI risks are everyday harms, namely scams that target seniors. He gives no catastrophic framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He talks about raising awareness of AI scams but does not endorse or oppose any AI rules or legislation.

members.summary: Vicente Gonzalez mentions AI mainly in local economic and consumer-protection terms. He sees it as a possible driver of jobs and industry, for example around the Corpus Christi naval air station. He also warns about AI-enabled scams that target seniors. He has not taken a clear stance on AI regulation, AGI, or China in these statements.

members.name: Jodey C. Arrington

just.ai_overall: He presents AI mainly as an economic and fiscal opportunity: productivity, growth, and savings. He acknowledges that risk needs managing, which suggests risks are manageable rather than dominant. He stops short of the unqualified enthusiasm that would earn a 4.
just.agi_pilled: He talks about AI as an economic and infrastructure boom, but no statement mentions AGI, superintelligence, or radical transformation on the scale of the industrial revolution.
just.x_risk: He mentions managing risk responsibly and says zero risk is impossible, but he names no catastrophic, existential, or loss-of-control risks, and he does not reject them either.
just.china_race: He repeatedly frames AI as a race the US must win, including 'America - not China - will lead', and calls winning an 'imperative'. He pairs this with a nod to managing risk, but the race is the main lens, and he cites it to favor an innovation-first posture.
just.regulation: He favors 'erring on the side of innovation' and says demanding zero risk means losing. He allows only for 'managing the risk responsibly', and he proposes no specific rules, which points to a light-touch stance.

members.summary: Arrington describes AI mainly as an engine of economic growth, government efficiency, and local investment, especially data center and energy development in West Texas. He frames AI as a race the US must win against China, and he favors an innovation-first posture with responsible risk management and no detailed regulatory proposals. He does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Pramila Jayapal

just.ai_overall: She frames AI mainly as a threat: economic collapse risk, deaths linked to chatbots, surveillance, discrimination, and possible harm to humanity. She grants in one quote that the technology could be used for good, but harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is too big and powerful to leave alone and calls for a 'seismic shift.' She refers to superintelligent systems but also says the industry uses 'superintelligence' framing to dodge responsibility. This signals significant transformation without clear AGI-timeline thinking.
just.x_risk: She says researchers warn AI 'could destroy humanity.' She cites systems that could 'kill us all,' calls for bans on models that 'go rogue' or create 'catastrophic risks,' and backs a government kill switch. She treats loss of control as real, though she also says the industry exploits 'rogue' framing to avoid responsibility.
just.china_race: She calls for working with China on global AI regulation and does not frame AI as a race to win. She uses 'race' only to describe companies' 'race to the bottom.'
just.regulation: She is proposing a comprehensive National AI Charter that would require licensing of all AI companies. It includes pre-approval, federal testing, bans on risky models, a kill switch, structural separation, and criminal penalties. She also backs a data center moratorium and opposes preemption of state laws.

members.summary: Pramila Jayapal speaks about AI almost entirely in terms of harm, corporate power, and accountability. She cites chatbot-linked deaths, surveillance, discrimination, economic fragility, and catastrophic or rogue-AI risk. She has introduced a sweeping licensing-style 'National AI Charter' and the AI Civil Rights Act, opposes preemption of state laws, and favors cooperating with China on global rules. She acknowledges potential benefits only briefly.

members.name: Ron Estes

just.ai_overall: The only statement is a brief congratulation to Wichita State that lists AI among fields of innovation. It gives no real view of AI's benefits or risks.
just.agi_pilled: Nothing in the statement addresses AGI, transformative AI, or expected scale of change.
just.x_risk: The statement does not discuss any AI risks, catastrophic or ordinary.
just.china_race: China and international competition are not mentioned.
just.regulation: The statement says nothing about AI regulation or policy.

members.summary: The only statement is a 2020 web post praising Wichita State researchers for a NASA award. It mentions artificial intelligence in passing, alongside flight and space exploration, as an area of innovation. It gives no view on AI risks, policy, or competition.

members.name: Ralph Norman

just.ai_overall: He says AI is 'a good thing and a bad thing,' with potential for a lot of damage, and he also backs using machine learning in medicine. He calls it too powerful and wants it kept from derailing the country, so he reads as balanced and somewhat cautious.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'coming wave of technology' but never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or a transformation on the scale of the industrial revolution. That is not enough to place him on this dimension.
just.x_risk: He says AI could 'derail the country' and is 'too powerful,' but he stays vague and cites concrete harms such as voice and image imitation and harm to children. He does not discuss catastrophic misuse or loss of control.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He says Congress will have to put guardrails in place and that we should 'regulate what you can,' particularly to protect children. He also emphasizes state and local control over data centers, and he gives no sign of backing a broad framework.

members.summary: Ralph Norman describes AI as both good and bad, a powerful 'coming wave' that could do a lot of damage if it is not handled well. His concerns center on deepfakes and voice imitation, children's safety, and local effects of data centers. He supports congressional guardrails and state and local control, and he says the subject is complex. He has said little about AGI or China.

members.name: Jimmy Gomez
